title: Implement query-driven fixup substituting classified calls with libc:: paths
description:
Consume the substitution table from slate-4wl9.1. For each confirmed
substitutable symbol, extend src/function_identity.rs's Known/classify_function
(or an adjacent classification keyed the same way) so calls to it are
identifiable at fixup time via the existing Provenance::TrustedHeader path -
do not build a new provenance mechanism, the CallBinding::Direct { identity,
.. } facts already carry what's needed.

Add a query-driven fixup under src/fixups/query/ (per
docs/writing-a-query-fixup.md) with a FnCall rule matching calls whose
identity is one of the newly-classified Known variants, rewriting the call
target to libc::<symbol> and dropping the now-dead shim-lowered extern "C"
item when nothing else in the translation unit still references it. Follow
docs/writing-a-fixup.md's AST-to-AST rule - no string rewriting.

Per this project's rule that correctness lives in baseline lowering: this
fixup must be strictly optional. With it disabled, the baseline
shim-lowered extern "C" declaration (today's behavior) must still be correct
Rust, just non-portable across libc/arch - the fixup only changes
*idiomaticity/portability*, never introduces new correctness.
acceptance_criteria:
Every symbol confirmed substitutable in slate-4wl9.1's table is classified
and rewritten by the fixup when called. New differential fixtures exist for
at least: a plain function substitution, a varargs substitution (ioctl), and
a constant substitution, each passing identically with the fixup enabled and
disabled (disabled = today's shim-lowered baseline). cargo fmt, cargo
clippy, and cargo nextest r --release all pass. No shim header or baseline
lowering path is removed - only the fixup's new output changes.

title: Audit libc-shim symbols for ABI-compatible libc:: crate equivalents
description:
Walk libc-shim's declared functions and object-like constants (pthread.h,
fenv.h, stdint.h limits, ioctl and friends, etc.) and check each against the
`libc` crate's exports for Slate's supported matrix: {x86_64, aarch64} x
{gnu, musl}. For each symbol, record whether libc:: exposes a
signature/ABI-compatible item (same param/return types after accounting for
Slate's C-to-Rust type lowering, same layout for any struct/typedef
involved), and any per-target divergence libc:: already encodes that the
shim currently hand-splits with #if defined(__SLATE_LIBC_GNU)/#elif
__SLATE_LIBC_MUSL (ioctl's second parameter is the motivating case: unsigned
long on glibc, int on musl).

Produce a table (symbol -> libc:: path, or "no match" + reason) covering at
minimum every symbol the shim currently #if-splits by libc, plus the
pthread_* and fenv_t-family symbols touched this session. Do not modify any
shim headers or lowering code in this task - this is a research/audit task
whose output is the substitution table plus a short note per unmatched
symbol explaining why (missing from libc::, incompatible layout, Slate-only
semantics, etc.).
acceptance_criteria: A written substitution table exists (symbol, libc:: path or none, verification notes) covering every currently-#if-split libc-shim symbol and the pthread_*/fenv_t symbols from this session; every entry is checked against actual libc crate source/docs, not assumed from memory.

title: Fixup: substitute libc-shim symbol calls with libc:: crate equivalents
description:
Slate currently hand-rolls every libc-shim declaration's Rust lowering as a
literal unsafe extern "C" block with the exact signature the shim gave CIR
(see libc-shim/include/pthread.h's ioctl split between __SLATE_LIBC_GNU and
__SLATE_LIBC_MUSL). Making that portable across libc/arch today means either
hand-writing a #[cfg(...)] block per divergent symbol, or building a
multi-config-diff engine that reruns the CIR frontend per target and merges
declarations - both are work Slate would be redoing that the `libc` crate
(already a dependency of generated output - see lower.rs's libc::c_char,
libc::timespec, libc::mbstate_t) has already solved, target-by-target, for
every function/constant it exports.

Add a fixup pass that, for calls whose function identity is already
classified as coming from a trusted libc-shim header (see
src/function_identity.rs's Provenance::TrustedHeader + Known enum, already
used to recognize e.g. qsort/bsearch/pthread_create/memcpy), rewrites the
call to reference libc::<symbol> instead of the shim-lowered extern "C" item,
when a curated audit confirms libc:: exports an ABI/signature-compatible
equivalent for Slate's supported (arch, libc) matrix (x86_64/aarch64 x
gnu/musl).

This does not replace libc-shim: CIR still needs the shim's concrete
declarations/struct layouts to parse and type-check the C input in the first
place (sizeof, field offsets, etc. all need real facts at parse time). This
fixup only changes what gets emitted for calls whose target has a trustworthy
libc:: counterpart, per docs/writing-a-fixup.md's rule that correctness lives
in baseline lowering - disabling this fixup must still leave correct,
shim-lowered Rust behind.
acceptance_criteria:
A curated table of libc-shim symbols with a confirmed ABI-compatible libc::
equivalent exists, with each entry's signature verified against the `libc`
crate for the full (x86_64/aarch64 x gnu/musl) matrix and any caveats
(varargs, differing request/flag types like ioctl's second parameter)
recorded. Symbols without a confirmed match are left on the baseline
shim-lowered path and are not silently substituted. The fixup pass rewrites
only calls classified via the existing FunctionIdentity/Known machinery,
never introduces a libc:: reference for an unclassified or ambiguous call,
and disabling the fixup still produces correct (if non-portable) Rust.
Differential fixtures cover at least one function-call substitution, one
varargs substitution (e.g. ioctl), and one constant substitution, each
passing identically pre- and post-fixup. cargo fmt/clippy/nextest all pass.

title: Facts: out-parameter allocation summary (T** write detection)
description: Cover the second common ownership-transfer shape: a function that allocates and hands ownership back through a T** parameter instead of a return value, e.g. void alloc(int **x) { *x = malloc(sizeof(int) * 10); } called as alloc(&x);. This is a distinct, common C idiom (many library-style APIs use a return code for status and an out-param for the allocated object) and needs its own detection path -- slate-knus.1's callee-allocation-summary only scans Stmt::Return, which finds nothing here since alloc() returns void. Requires the collector to query a function's PARAMETERS (FnDef.params), not just its return statements -- generalizing 'where can this function hand off a fresh allocation' from one exit shape (return) to two (return, out-param write).
design:
New collector (or a second pass alongside slate-knus.1's, sharing the malloc/peel_casts/extent detection helpers, not duplicating them) that scans FnDef.params for a parameter whose ty is Type::Ptr{inner: Type::Ptr{inner: elem_ty, ..}, ..} (T**), then checks the body for an unconditional *param = malloc(...)-sourced write (same is_malloc_call/extent_from_malloc_size logic as the return-value path) with no intervening free or reassignment before every path returns. Keep the same single-consistent-site discipline as slate-knus.1 -- conditional or multiple write sites are out of scope for the first cut. Judge each qualifying T** parameter independently -- a function with several out-parameters (void alloc(int **x, int **y)) can have some convert and others not, since nothing about one parameter's conversion depends on another's.

Note for whichever ticket eventually rewrites this shape (not this ticket -- facts only): the Rust target is NOT a return value. void alloc(int **x, int **y) does not fit fn alloc() -> Vec<T> at all once there is more than one out-parameter -- bundling into a tuple return (-> (Vec<T>, Vec<U>)) forces an all-or-nothing decision across every out-param in the function, which breaks the independent per-parameter eligibility this ticket's facts are designed to support. The correct target keeps the same parameter position and count, just retypes it: fn alloc(x: &mut Vec<i32>, y: &mut Vec<i32>) { *x = vec![0; 10]; *y = vec![0; 5]; }, with call sites changing alloc(&x, &y); to alloc(&mut x, &mut y);, and x/y themselves declared as let mut x: Vec<i32> = Vec::new(); (a zero-allocation placeholder, exactly analogous to the Option<Box<T>> = None placeholder slate-04q.83.4's OptionBoxLocals pass already uses) before the call -- there is no 'was x initialized' question since this ticket only detects UNCONDITIONAL out-param writes, so alloc() always overwrites *x before returning regardless of its pre-call value. The eventual rewrite ticket needs the same cross-function atomicity as slate-knus.3's EditSet but a per-parameter edit shape (retype one parameter + one call-site argument at a time, independently), not slate-knus.4's whole-signature return-type change.
acceptance_criteria: A fixture with void alloc(int **x) { *x = malloc(sizeof(int) * 10); } produces an owning summary keyed to the out-parameter: elem_ty=i32, extent=Count(10), transferred via parameter index 0. A fixture where the out-param write is conditional (if (cond) *x = malloc(...);) does not produce a summary. A fixture where *x is also freed or reassigned before return does not produce a summary. A single-pointer parameter passed by value (void alloc(int *x) { x = malloc(...); } -- the caller never sees the write, this is a real C bug, not an ownership-transfer idiom) must NOT be misdetected as an out-parameter allocator. Facts collector covered by fixture-driven differential tests per docs/adding-features.md.

title: Rewrite: interprocedural Box<T>/Vec<T> promotion for simple allocator functions
description: Wire the callee-allocation-summary fact, the caller-eligibility join, and the multi-function EditSet together into an actual rewrite pass: int *alloc(void) { return malloc(sizeof(int) * N); }, used only by callers with eligible local usage, gets alloc()'s return type promoted to Vec<T> (or Box<T> for N==1 / scalar), with every caller's binding type updated in the same atomic edit. This is the first end-to-end ticket in the epic -- .1-.3 build the capability, this ticket ships the first working case.
design: Depends on the callee-allocation-summary, caller-eligibility-join, and multi-function-EditSet tickets. New Pass:: variant placed after Pass::HeapOwnership (reuses its recipe helpers -- box_new/vec construction -- rather than re-deriving them). Scope narrowly for the first cut: single direct-call allocator functions with exactly the shape in this epic's acceptance criteria; do not attempt indirect calls, function pointers, or allocator functions with multiple malloc sites on this pass.
acceptance_criteria: Fixture: int *alloc(void) { return malloc(sizeof(int) * 10); } int main(void) { int *x = NULL; x = alloc(); x[0] = 10; printf("%d\n", x[0]); return 0; } recovers alloc()'s return type to Vec<i32> and main()'s x to Vec<i32>, with x[0] = 10; as safe indexing (no unsafe). Negative fixture: same shape but the caller does raw pointer arithmetic on the result -- both functions stay baseline raw-pointer Rust, byte for byte. Full cargo nextest r --release passes.
notes:
Follow-up: the pass-through wrapper limitation documented at close time
("real, separate follow-on work -- not attempted here") is now resolved.
Multi-level chains (alloc() -> indirect() -> main(), and deeper) now promote
correctly in one atomic edit.

Root cause of the gap: a pass-through caller (fn indirect() { alloc() }, no
named local binding) was never recognized as a "caller" at all by the
eligibility scan, which only matched the null-decl-then-call-then-assign
shape. So alloc() was rejected outright for having zero recognized callers,
even though it was safely used transitively through indirect().

Fixed with an architecture cleanup along the way, not just a bolted-on
third fact (per direct user feedback questioning exactly that approach):
CalleeAllocSummaryFact (.1) is now a genuine provenance union --
AllocProvenance::Direct{elem_ty, extent, ...} for a function whose return
traces to a real malloc/calloc call, or AllocProvenance::PassThrough
{callee_name} for a function whose return is just a call to another
function. Both branches are detected by the same intraprocedural collector
(.1 already had all the return-shape-matching logic; it only needed a
second arm). The interprocedural side (.2) no longer duplicates that
detection -- it walks .1's provenance facts via a visited-set-guarded
resolve_root helper, and the wrapper chain (every pass-through function
between a caller and its ultimate allocator) falls out of that walk as a
Vec<FunctionId> field directly on the existing InterproceduralAllocEligibilityFact,
not a separate fact type. The eligibility conjunction now checks every real
caller across every function in the resolved chain, not just the root.
The rewrite rule (.4) fetches the chain via a new interprocedural_alloc_chain
query and retypes every wrapper's return type (body unchanged -- a
pass-through's `return alloc();` stays exactly correct once alloc() itself
returns Vec<T>) as part of the same atomic multi-function EditSet.

Also accommodates the free()-optionality being reverted (each fixture must
now include an explicit free() call, matching heap_ownership.rs's original
strict requirement, undoing this ticket's earlier require_free relaxation).

Added tests/fixtures/interprocedural_alloc_promotion_chain.c (two-level
indirection) plus a matching differential + structural test. Manually
verified three-level chains and a pure two-function pass-through cycle
(f() { g() } / g() { f() }, neither with an independent allocation) resolve
to "leave both as raw pointers" without hanging, exercising the visited-set
guard on the new resolve_root walk specifically (not just accidentally
rejected by an unrelated check).

Full cargo fmt / cargo clippy --release --all-targets /
cargo nextest r --release (221 passed, 2 skipped) all green.
close_reason:
First end-to-end interprocedural rewrite in the epic: int *alloc(void) {
return malloc(sizeof(int) * N); } used only by callers with eligible local
usage now recovers alloc()'s return type to Vec<T> (or Box<T> for a scalar
allocation), with every caller's binding retyped and every use-site
converted to safe indexing/deref in the same atomic multi-function edit.

Design: wired slate-knus.1's callee-allocation-summary,
slate-knus.2's caller-eligibility-join, and slate-knus.3's proven multi-item
EditSet primitive together. New Pass::InterproceduralAllocPromotion runs
right after Pass::OptionBoxLocals (same position as heap_ownership.rs,
before Pass::DeadLocals). Reused heap_ownership.rs's existing use-rewriting
engine wholesale rather than reimplementing pointer-arithmetic-to-indexing
conversion: bumped OwnedHeap/OwnedHeapPlan/rewrite_owned_stmt (the
structural, name+kind-driven leaf rewriter that converts *p.add(i) -> p[i]
and unwraps the now-redundant unsafe wrapping as part of the same walk) and
added a new OwnedHeap::from_owners constructor so the caller-side rewrite
doesn't need to fabricate an unrelated HeapOwnershipPlan just to build one.
Did NOT reuse heap_ownership.rs's own orchestrator (rewrite_owned_body_stmts/
ownership_plan) -- it's tightly coupled to malloc/free-shaped flat
statement-index bookkeeping (pointer decl must be a top-level Stmt::Let,
calloc-count assumed at allocation_stmt-2, etc.) that doesn't fit a
call-sourced allocation. Wrote a new, much smaller orchestrator instead
(rewrite_interprocedural_alloc_callee/rewrite_interprocedural_alloc_caller
in recipe.rs) that only handles the declaration retyping and
alias/free-statement bookkeeping this shape actually needs, then hands off
to the shared leaf rewriter for every use site.

Two real bugs found and fixed along the way, both surfaced only once an
actual end-to-end fixture was run through the full pipeline (not caught by
any prior ticket's own testing, since neither .1 nor .2 exercised a real
rewrite):

1. The ticket's own required fixture -- x[0] = 10; printf(...); return 0;
   with no free(x) call at all -- was being rejected outright:
   heap_uses_are_owned (reused from heap_ownership.rs for the caller-side
   eligibility check) hard-requires a matching free() call
   (let (free_index, free_temp) = free?;), a requirement heap_ownership.rs's
   own pass genuinely needs (its Box/Vec is meant to REPLACE an explicit
   malloc/free pair) but that doesn't apply here -- the callee already fully
   owns the allocation lifecycle via Vec's/Box's Drop, whether or not the
   caller happens to free it explicitly. Made the free requirement an
   explicit require_free: bool parameter (heap_ownership.rs's own call site
   passes true, preserving its exact existing behavior byte for byte; the
   new interprocedural caller-eligibility check passes false). Also had to
   widen OwnedHeapUses's free_index from usize to Option<usize> to carry the
   "no free found" case through, and thread the resulting read_safety value
   into the caller-eligibility fact -- .2's own collector had been silently
   discarding it, but it's required to decide Vec vs Box the same way
   heap_ownership.rs's own ownership_plan does (Elements-extent with
   MayReadUninitialized read_safety must reject the whole conversion, not
   just fall back to raw pointers, matching the existing rule's own
   discipline).

2. .1's CalleeAllocSummaryFact never recorded where the malloc call itself
   lives (only the return statement), so there was no way to remove it once
   the return got replaced with vec![0; N] -- this is exactly the same
   "leftover malloc call executes and leaks" class of bug found and fixed
   earlier in slate-04q.83.4. Added alloc_source_path to the fact (the
   malloc-temp's own Let statement, already located internally by the
   collector via find_temp_index but previously discarded) and removed that
   statement as part of the callee rewrite; verified generated output has
   zero remaining malloc calls or extern declarations once nothing else
   references it.

Scope, matching the ticket's own "single direct-call allocator functions"
framing: only functions with a DIRECT slate-knus.1 base-case summary get
rewritten -- pass-through wrapper functions that only qualify via
slate-knus.2's recursive resolution (return g();) are correctly left
untouched by this ticket (case.fact(query.callee_alloc_summary(function))
rejects them, since they have no base-case summary). Rewriting those too is
real, separate follow-on work (their own return type needs updating, but
their body needs no other change since forwarding a Vec<T>/Box<T> value is
already valid) -- not attempted here, consistent with "do not attempt ...
on this pass" in the ticket's design note.

Verified both required fixtures via full differential (compile + run both
C and Rust, compare stdout/exit code) in addition to structural assertions:
tests/fixtures/interprocedural_alloc_promotion.c (positive -- alloc()
becomes Vec<i32>, x[0] = 10 is safe indexing, zero remaining unsafe/malloc)
and tests/fixtures/interprocedural_alloc_promotion_arith_bailout.c
(negative -- pointer arithmetic on the result correctly blocks the whole
conversion, both functions stay byte-for-byte raw-pointer baseline). Added
matching structural tests in tests/differential.rs.

title: Engine: multi-function atomic EditSet for cross-function rewrites
description: QueryRule<Function>/EditSet today opens one transactional edit per function. Interprocedural promotion needs to change a callee's signature + body AND every caller's call-site + binding type together, atomically -- doing it in separate per-function edits risks a state where alloc() returns Vec<i32> but a caller's binding is still typed *mut i32, a type error the pipeline would emit without ever noticing until rustc rejects it (or a differential run does).
design: New rule shape in src/fixups/query/item.rs (ItemPlanBuilder/EditSet) that can name a SET of functions (the callee plus every caller from the caller-eligibility ticket's conjunction) and open one EditSet spanning all of them, following the existing 'never leave the binding's declared type and its use sites inconsistent mid-pass' transactional principle from writing-a-query-fixup.md, just widened from one function's body to N functions' bodies. Related to slate-04q.75.56's broader query/rewrite engine generalization (statement-window matching, memoization) -- coordinate with that work rather than duplicating engine-generalization effort; this ticket does not require slate-04q.75.56 to complete first.
acceptance_criteria: A rule can request edits touching alloc()'s FnDef (signature + body) and every caller's FnDef (call-site + binding type) as one EditSet; if any single sub-edit in the set is rejected (e.g. a caller's binding type can't be resolved), the WHOLE set is rejected and nothing is applied -- no partial cross-function state. Existing single-function QueryRule usages are unaffected (no regression in the current heap_ownership.rs / option_box_locals.rs rules). Full cargo nextest r --release passes.
close_reason:
Key finding, which substantially changes this ticket's scope from what the
epic's design note assumed: the multi-function atomic EditSet primitive
already exists in src/fixups/query/item.rs. An EditSet is Vec<AnchoredEdit>,
and each AnchoredEdit variant (Function/Expression/Statement/etc.) carries
its own item_index -- nothing in the type requires all edits in a set to
target the same item. The overlap checker (anchors_overlap) already compares
item_index before flagging a collision, so edits in different functions
never spuriously conflict; the per-set validation (missing_targets) already
checks every anchor in a set against the pristine program before any
mutation and drops the WHOLE set if any anchor is stale; and the appliers
(apply_function_edits, apply_statement_edits, etc.) already iterate their
edit lists independently by item_index with no single-item assumption
anywhere. src/fixups/query/rules/unused_params.rs is already-shipped,
already-tested (via its own e2e fixture) production evidence of exactly this
shape: it builds one EditSet containing a Function-anchor replacement of the
callee PLUS an Expression-anchor edit at every call site, which may live in
different functions than the callee -- proving the "callee signature change
+ N callers' edits, atomic or nothing" pattern this epic needs already works
end to end.

Given that, this ticket's actual gap was narrower than its own design note
implied: not missing engine machinery, but missing test coverage proving the
specific "Function-anchor replace in one item + Statement-anchor edit in a
DIFFERENT item, same EditSet" shape behaves atomically -- item.rs's existing
unit test suite (missing_target_rejects_the_complete_edit_set,
mixed_edits_use_snapshot_paths_and_report_one_atomic_application, etc.) only
ever exercised single-item programs, and none of them used an
AnchoredEdit::Function anchor at all (constructing a valid FunctionRef needs
a real FunctionId from facts::analyze, which the existing test helpers never
did). Function-kind edits had zero unit coverage despite being
production-used by heap_ownership.rs, option_box_locals.rs, and
unused_params.rs.

Added two new unit tests to item.rs's existing #[cfg(test)] module (this
file's own established convention for engine-level plumbing that has no
C source to differentially test against):
- function_edit_and_statement_edit_in_a_different_item_apply_atomically:
  a 2-function program, one EditSet containing a Function-anchor replace of
  item 1 ("callee") and a Statement-anchor edit of item 0 ("caller"); both
  land together in one apply() call.
- stale_anchor_in_one_item_rejects_the_whole_multi_item_set: same shape but
  the Statement anchor points at an out-of-range statement index; asserts
  the program is byte-for-byte unchanged (including item 1's otherwise-valid
  Function replacement, which does NOT partially apply), report.applied == 0,
  and a MissingTarget diagnostic is recorded.

Also added a named_function(name, body) test helper (the existing function()
helper hardcoded name: "test", which can't build a two-function program with
distinguishable targets) and a function_ref(facts, item_index, name) helper
that resolves a real FunctionId via facts.function_by_item_index(item_index)
against an analyzed program, since FunctionRef's id field is only
constructible with a genuine FunctionId, not hand-rolled.

No changes needed to AnchoredEdit, the planner's overlap logic, or any
apply_*_edits function -- all of it already handled this correctly. No new
convenience mutator (e.g. push_replace_function) was added either: the
epic's actual need (one Function anchor for the promoted callee plus
Statement/Expression anchors for each caller) is fully served by
EditSet::replace_function(...) followed by push_replace_statement/
push_replace_expression, exactly as unused_params.rs already does it and as
the new tests now directly verify at the engine level.

title: Facts: interprocedural caller-eligibility join (visited-set guarded)
description: Extend the existing local heap-use/pointer_option_eligible checks so a candidate pointer's source can be a call to a function carrying an owning summary (from the callee-allocation-summary ticket), not just a direct malloc call. Add the caller-side conjunction: whether a callee's OWN signature can convert is the AND, over every caller found via direct_calls(function), of that caller's local eligibility check on its own use of the call's result.
design: Reuse CallRecord{target: CallTarget::Direct(name), ..} (forward edge: caller -> callee, resolved via all_functions()) and direct_calls(function) (reverse edge: callee -> every caller) -- both already exist in query/context.rs, built for reachability/inlining. No new call-graph data structure. Walk via ordinary recursive queries; query_cache! memoization handles the DAG. Guard recursion with a visited-set (functions currently being resolved) rather than fixed-point iteration: mark a function in-progress on entry to its eligibility computation; if resolution re-enters an in-progress function (a call cycle), return 'not proven' for that inner lookup only, not an error. This is sound (the safe default is always 'leave as raw pointer') and exact for pass-through-only cycles; it only loses precision when one side of a cycle has an independent proof a full fixed point would propagate through -- documented, accepted gap, not solved here.
acceptance_criteria: Given int *alloc(void) { return malloc(sizeof(int) * 10); } and a single caller that only indexes/derefs the result, the caller-eligibility check passes and the conjunction over direct_calls(alloc) is satisfied. Adding a second caller that does raw pointer arithmetic on alloc()'s result flips the conjunction to false for alloc(). A mutually recursive pair (f calls g, g calls f) where neither independently proves ownership resolves to 'not owned' via the visited-set guard without hanging. Facts/query layer covered by fixture-driven differential tests.
close_reason:
Implemented the interprocedural caller-eligibility join: whether a function
F's signature can convert is the conjunction, over every caller found by
scanning the whole program, of that caller's local use of F()'s result being
compatible with Box<T>/Vec<T> semantics.

Split into two pieces during implementation, since the ticket's own acceptance
criteria (a mutually recursive pass-through pair) turned out to require the
recursion to live in a different place than the description first suggested:

1. Extended, recursive "resolved allocation summary" (new, beyond what the
   ticket description names but required by its own third acceptance
   criterion): slate-knus.1's CalleeAllocSummaryFact only recognizes a
   function whose return traces to a DIRECT malloc/calloc call. A
   pass-through wrapper (`int *wrapper(void) { return alloc(); }`) has no
   such summary at all under .1's intentionally-intraprocedural scope. Added
   resolve_summary(name, ..., visited): base case is .1's existing summary;
   recursive case is "the function's one and only top-level return is
   Expr::Call{func: Var(other_name), ..} to another user-defined function,
   and THAT function (recursively) has a summary too, which gets inherited."
   Verified empirically first (via a temporary PRE_HEAP-adjacent debug dump)
   that `return alloc();` does NOT get hoisted into a temp the way
   `x = alloc();` does -- baseline lowering only hoists call results when
   they're assigned to a named binding, not when directly returned -- so the
   recursive case matches Stmt::Return's expr directly, no temp-name lookup
   needed, simpler than the base case.

   Cycle guard: a plain visited-set (BTreeSet<String>) threaded through the
   recursion, per the ticket's design note -- NOT fixed-point iteration.
   Re-entering a function already in the set returns None for that lookup.
   Verified this resolves a genuine cycle (f() { return g(); } / g() {
   return f(); }, neither with an independent malloc) to "no summary for
   either" without hanging -- confirmed by timeout-wrapped run completing
   normally with zero eligibility facts produced for f or g.

2. Local caller-eligibility check, reusing heap_ownership.rs's own
   heap_uses_are_owned wholesale (bumped Candidate, OwnedHeapUses,
   heap_uses_are_owned, null_pointer_decl, and assigns_allocated_pointer from
   private to pub(super)) rather than reimplementing use-classification
   logic that already correctly distinguishes safe indexed/scalar
   read-write from disqualifying raw pointer arithmetic (via
   reassigns_pointer's fallback rejection) and already requires a matching
   free() call. The only new code is finding the call-sourced allocation
   site itself (call_allocation_temp/find_call_allocation, mirroring
   heap_ownership.rs's own allocation_temp/find_allocation but matching
   "Let-bound temp from a call to a resolved-summary function" instead of
   "Let-bound temp from malloc/calloc").

New InterproceduralAllocEligibilityFact (facts/mod.rs), collected in
src/fixups/facts/interprocedural_alloc_eligibility.rs, exposed via a new
per-function interprocedural_alloc_eligibility(function) query in
query/context.rs -- #[allow(dead_code)] until slate-knus.4 consumes it,
matching the same facts-only pattern as slate-knus.1.

Verified against all three of the ticket's stated scenarios: single caller
indexing/dereffing only -> eligible=true; adding a second caller doing raw
pointer arithmetic -> eligible=false; a pure pass-through cycle -> no summary
for either function, run completes without hanging. All three checked via a
temporary debug dump placed at the exact point right before Pass::HeapOwnership
runs (removed before finishing) -- NOT by printing on every facts::analyze()
call throughout the pipeline. That distinction mattered: an unrelated,
later-running fold pass (something like "zero-init declarations fold into
their overwriting assignment") legitimately simplifies away the
null_pointer_decl-then-separate-assign shape this ticket's detection depends
on, once nothing has consumed it first -- which is exactly what happens on
every snapshot after Pass::HeapOwnership since there's no consuming rule yet.
Printing on every analyze() call initially showed spurious "eligible=true"
results from those later snapshots (the scan finds nothing at all once the
shape is gone, so the conjunction is vacuously true) that had nothing to do
with the actual logic -- same "comparing facts across different pipeline
snapshots produces spurious mismatches" trap from earlier tickets in this
epic. Confirmed correct by checking specifically at the snapshot right after
Pass::HeapOwnership, matching where a real consuming rule would run.

Full cargo fmt / cargo clippy --release --all-targets /
cargo nextest r --release (216 passed, 2 skipped, unchanged since nothing
consumes the new fact yet) all green.

title: Facts: callee allocation summary (return-value ownership detection)
description: Compute, per function, whether every return path proves a fresh, ownership-transferring heap allocation with a consistent elem_ty/extent -- e.g. int *alloc(void) { return malloc(sizeof(int) * 10); }. Purely intraprocedural: reuses heap_ownership.rs's existing find_allocation/extent_from_malloc_size logic, retargeted from Stmt::Let inits to Stmt::Return expressions. Zero call-graph traversal in this ticket -- it only reads the function's own body.
design: New fact, keyed by plain FunctionId (not (FunctionId, AstPath) like most current facts) since it's a whole-function property. Every return path must agree on elem_ty and a consistent HeapExtent (matching heap_ownership's existing single-allocation-site discipline) or the function is not a candidate. A function with zero return statements, or any return path that doesn't trace to a fresh malloc/calloc with no intervening free, is not a candidate. Reuse int_value/type_size_bytes/extent_from_malloc_size/extent_from_calloc_args as-is; do not re-derive extent math.
acceptance_criteria: A fixture with int *alloc(void) { return malloc(sizeof(int) * 10); } produces a summary fact: owns=true, elem_ty=i32, extent=Count(10). A fixture with a conditional return (if (x) return malloc(...); else return NULL;) does not produce an owning summary (inconsistent path). A fixture that mallocs but also frees before returning does not produce an owning summary. Facts collector covered by fixture-driven differential tests per docs/adding-features.md.
close_reason:
Implemented the callee allocation-summary fact: per function, does every
return path prove a fresh, ownership-transferring allocation with a
consistent elem_ty/extent. Purely intraprocedural per the ticket's scope --
zero call-graph traversal, reads only the function's own body.

Verified the exact baseline-lowering shape empirically before writing the
collector (via a temporary PRE_HEAP debug dump, removed before finishing):
malloc/calloc calls always get hoisted into a temp let
(`let _v3 = unsafe { malloc(...) };`) even inside a function whose C source
directly writes `return malloc(...);`, and the return statement itself stays
a literal `Stmt::Return`, not a tail expression -- so the detection shape is
"exactly one Stmt::Return anywhere in the function, found at the function
body's top level, whose (cast-peeled) expr is a bare Var naming a temp that
was itself just defined via the same malloc/calloc-call shape
heap_ownership.rs already recognizes."

Implementation: new src/fixups/facts/callee_alloc_summary.rs. Bumped
heap_ownership.rs's private allocation_temp()/AllocationCall (and the fields
this ticket needs: name, kind, extent, init) to pub(super) and reused them
as-is rather than re-deriving the malloc/calloc-size/extent math, per the
ticket's design note. New CalleeAllocSummaryFact keyed by plain FunctionId
(facts/mod.rs), collected via the same program-items loop pattern as every
other collector, and exposed through a new per-function
callee_alloc_summary(function) query in query/context.rs (matching how
slate-04q.83.2/.3 exposed their facts before a consuming rule existed --
new Predicate::CalleeAllocSummary/EvidenceDetail variant, #[allow(dead_code)]
until slate-knus.2 consumes it).

Scope, deliberately narrow, matching every other ticket in this epic's
"leave as baseline/reject rather than partially handle" discipline:
- Requires the function have exactly one Stmt::Return in its ENTIRE body
  (any nesting depth) and that one return must be a top-level statement of
  the function body, not nested in any if/else/loop. A function with a
  conditional return (if (x) return malloc(...); else return NULL;) has two
  nested returns and zero top-level ones -- rejected on both counts
  independently, not specially handled.
- The return's traced temp must be the malloc/calloc call's own hoisted
  temp directly. A named local that got malloc'd then freed then returned
  (int *p = malloc(...); free(p); return p;) is rejected too, but as a side
  effect of not recognizing the indirection at all (p's own declaration is a
  NULL-decl, not a malloc-shaped let) -- not via explicit free-tracking. This
  is a real narrowing versus a fuller "track uses between allocation and
  return like heap_uses_are_owned does for the assignment case" -- accepted
  as a documented gap since the ticket's stated fixtures don't need it, not
  discovered as an oversight.

Verification methodology: this ticket has no consuming rule yet (that's
slate-knus.2/.4), so there is nothing observable in generated Rust to assert
on with the project's usual differential+structural-output tests -- matching
how slate-04q.83.2/.3 (facts-only, same epic pattern) shipped without
automated tests until a consumer existed. Verified instead via temporary
env-gated debug dumps of the collected fact (removed before finishing)
against six manual fixtures: direct malloc return (accepted, correct
elem_ty/extent/kind), calloc return (accepted, correct Zeroed init), the
ticket's two required negative fixtures (conditional return, malloc-then-
free-then-return -- both correctly produce no summary), a pure pass-through
function returning its own parameter (no summary), and a bare identity
function whose return is a block tail-expr rather than a Stmt::Return at all
(no summary, confirming the Stmt::Return-only match doesn't misfire on that
shape). Automated differential/structural tests will land with slate-knus.4
once this fact is consumed and observable.

title: Recover heap ownership across function boundaries (interprocedural Box<T>/Vec<T>)
description: heap_ownership.rs's malloc/free -> Box<T>/Vec<T> recovery is strictly intraprocedural: it only recognizes a malloc call and its uses within the SAME function body. A common, otherwise-trivial pattern is missed entirely: a helper function that allocates and returns ownership (e.g. int *alloc(void) { return malloc(sizeof(int) * 10); }), used by a caller that only ever treats the result as an owned buffer -- nothing converts, both stay raw *mut T. Nothing in the current facts or query layer is interprocedural: every fact is keyed by (FunctionId, AstPath) and every QueryRule operates on one function's body at a time. The underlying per-value eligibility checks (heap_ownership's own use-safety analysis) already answer the right local question -- what is missing is a way to connect a function's return value to its callers' uses.
design:
Split into two fact kinds rather than one 'interprocedural analysis' pass, per the design discussion this epic is transcribing:

(1) Callee allocation summary is PURELY intraprocedural: does F's body prove every return path yields a fresh, ownership-transferring allocation, with what elem_ty/extent. Computed by pointing today's find_allocation/extent_from_malloc_size logic at return statements instead of let-inits, independently per function, zero graph walking, keyed by plain FunctionId.

(2) Caller eligibility reuses today's local heap-use/pointer_option_eligible checks unchanged. The only extension: recognize a candidate whose source is a call to a function carrying an owning summary from (1), not just a direct malloc call.

The call-graph join these two need already exists in the query layer -- no new graph data structure required. CallRecord{target: CallTarget::Direct(name), ..} on every call site gives the forward edge (caller -> callee, resolved via all_functions()); direct_calls(function) already gives the reverse edge (callee -> every caller), used today for reachability/inlining decisions. Walk both directions via ordinary recursive queries; query_cache! memoization handles the DAG.

Deciding whether a callee's OWN signature can convert is the conjunction, over every caller found via direct_calls, of the caller-eligibility check from (2). Handle recursive/mutually-recursive calls with a VISITED-SET GUARD during the recursive descent (mark a function in-progress on entry; re-entering an in-progress function returns 'not proven' for that inner lookup only), NOT full fixed-point iteration to a lattice fixed point. This is sound: 'not proven' always resolves to the safe default (leave as raw pointer), matching every other pass in this codebase choosing a conservative bailout over new general machinery. It is exact, not approximate, for genuine pass-through-only cycles (f() { return g(); } / g() { return f(); }, no independent malloc anywhere) -- there is no real allocation reachable through infinite mutual pass-through, so 'not owned' is the TRUE answer there, not a conservative approximation. It only loses precision in the narrow case where one side of a cycle has an independent proof (its own malloc branch) that a full fixed point would eventually propagate through the cycle and a single guarded pass won't. Accepted as a known, documented gap -- not solved by this epic.

Applying an eligible conversion needs a primitive the engine does not have today: QueryRule<Function>/EditSet opens one transactional edit per function. This needs a rule that can open ONE atomic edit spanning the callee's signature + body AND every caller's call-site + binding type together -- get this wrong and you get 'let x: *mut i32 = alloc()' where alloc() now returns Vec<i32>, a type error. This is new work in src/fixups/query/item.rs's ItemPlanBuilder/EditSet, not an extension of the facts layer. Related to slate-04q.75.56's broader query/rewrite engine generalization (statement-window matching, memoization) -- sequence with awareness of that work rather than duplicating engine-generalization effort, though this epic does not depend on it completing first.
acceptance_criteria: int *alloc(void) { return malloc(sizeof(int) * N); } used by exactly one caller that only indexes/derefs the result safely recovers alloc()'s return type to Vec<T> (or Box<T> for a scalar single allocation) and updates the caller's binding type in the same atomic edit. A caller that does anything incompatible with Vec/Box (raw pointer arithmetic, storing into a raw-typed struct field, passing to a non-converted function) blocks the whole conversion -- both alloc() and every caller stay baseline raw-pointer Rust, never partially rewritten. A call cycle reachable from the candidate is detected via the visited-set guard and conservatively bails to baseline rather than hanging or panicking. Full cargo nextest r --release passes.

title: Rewrite: Option<Box<T>> recovery for tree-shaped struct fields (linked structures)
description:
Extends the Option<Box<T>> recovery to struct fields forming tree-shaped structures (linked lists, trees) once the whole-program struct_field_ownership facts exist. This is the harder, program-wide sibling of the locals/params/returns rewrite: a record's next/child field becomes Option<Box<Node>> only when struct_field_ownership_facts proves it tree-eligible (no back-pointers, no second incoming owning pointer, no cycle).

Explicit negative requirement from the parent epic: a doubly-linked list's prev field (or any field that fails the tree check) must be left completely untouched -- detected and excluded, never silently misclassified as Box.
design:
Register Pass::OptionBoxFields (string "option_box_fields") in src/fixups/trace.rs, stepped in src/fixups/mod.rs immediately after the locals ticket's Pass::OptionBoxLocals step -- struct-field recovery should see any local-variable Option<Box> rewrites that already landed, and reuses that ticket's recipe helpers (option_box_decl-style construction, guard-based deref rewriting) rather than duplicating them; factor shared pieces out of src/fixups/query/recipe.rs if the locals ticket didn't already leave them generically usable.

New rule file src/fixups/query/rules/option_box_fields.rs, QueryRule<WholeProgram> shape (matching rules/anonymous_structs.rs as the closest existing whole-program rewrite template, since this rewrites record definitions AND every access site together in one pass, not per-function).

1. case.fact(struct_field_ownership_facts()) from the prerequisite ticket; only proceed for fields marked tree-eligible.
2. For each eligible field, additionally require case.fact(pointer_option_eligible(...)) and case.fact(null_check_dominance(...)) at every p->field dereference site across the whole program -- reuse the exact same fact queries the locals ticket uses, do not add a second classification path.
3. Rewrite the record definition's field type (T *next -> Option<Box<T>>), every field-literal/assignment initializer, and every guarded access site (p->next non-null check -> if let Some(...) = &p.next, comparisons and NULL assignments per the same table as the locals ticket) as one EditSet::replace_program (per writing-a-query-fixup.md's Program rules section) so the type change and every use site move together atomically.
4. A field that fails struct_field_ownership_facts (the doubly-linked prev case, or any unproven incoming-edge count) must be left byte-for-byte as raw-pointer baseline -- this is the pass's primary regression risk, so the negative fixture matters as much as the positive one.

Fixtures (fixture-first, tests/fixtures/): a singly-linked or tree struct whose child/next field DOES get recovered to Option<Box<T>>, with a guarded deref exercising both is_some()/is_none() and if-let paths; and a doubly-linked struct (next + prev) that must NOT be rewritten at all -- assert the generated Rust still declares raw *mut fields for both. Same test-drive loop as the locals ticket (SLATE_DIFF_FIXTURE, then full cargo nextest r --release).
acceptance_criteria: New Pass::OptionBoxFields step runs after Pass::OptionBoxLocals, skippable via the optional fixup-runner boundary. Positive fixture: a singly-linked or tree struct's next/child field recovers to Option<Box<T>> with guarded is_some/is_none/if-let access. Negative fixture: a doubly-linked struct (next + prev) is left with both fields as raw *mut T, byte for byte -- struct_field_ownership_facts correctly rejects both. Full cargo nextest r --release passes.

title: Rewrite: Option<Box<T>> recovery for local/param/return heap-owned nullable pointers
description:
First end-to-end, user-visible rewrite in the epic: recover Option<Box<T>> for a LOCAL variable, function parameter, or return slot that is a heap-owned pointer which may legitimately be NULL at some point in its lifetime (as opposed to heap_ownership.rs's existing pass, which only handles the narrower "always allocated immediately after declaration, always freed" shape and rewrites straight to Box<T>/Vec<T> with no Option). Example shape: T *p = NULL; if (cond) { p = malloc(sizeof(T)); ... } if (p) { use(p); free(p); }.

Per the epic's design doc: correctness stays in baseline raw-pointer lowering; this fixup is a strict opt-in cleanup pass. Any pointer identity that fails an invariant (pointer_option_eligible, pointer_comparison_kind, or null_check_dominance from the two prerequisite fact tickets) is left exactly as baseline raw-pointer Rust -- not partially rewritten.

Scoped deliberately narrower than the parent epic's full acceptance criteria: locals/params/returns only. Struct-field trees (linked lists, doubly so) are the separate child ticket that reuses this ticket's rewrite recipe once struct_field_ownership facts exist.
design:
Register a new Pass::OptionBoxLocals variant in src/fixups/trace.rs (string "option_box_locals" per the existing naming convention) and a new step in src/fixups/mod.rs placed AFTER Pass::HeapOwnership's existing step (around line 638) -- this pass must run once heap_ownership's own Box/Vec rewrite has already stabilized its output, per the epic's invariant 5 note not to re-derive that classification.

New rule file src/fixups/query/rules/option_box_locals.rs, QueryRule<Function> shape (matching heap_ownership.rs's rule as the closest existing template). For each candidate binding whose declared type is a nullable pointer:
1. case.fact(pointer_option_eligible(binding)) from the prerequisite ticket -- reject if ineligible.
2. Identify the allocation/free lifecycle the same way heap_ownership.rs's ownership_plan does (reuse query.heap_ownership_facts(function) directly rather than re-deriving malloc/free recognition), but for THIS pass's target shape the pointer is not unconditionally assigned at declaration -- it starts NULL (or is a param/return slot that can be NULL).
3. case.fact(null_check_dominance(...)) from the prerequisite ticket for every deref site -- reject on any unproven deref.
4. Build the replacement via a new recipe function in src/fixups/query/recipe.rs, e.g. option_box_decl(...): decl type *mut T -> Option<Box<T>>; p = NULL -> p = None; p = malloc(...) (already Box::new(...) per heap_ownership) -> p = Some(Box::new(...)); p == NULL / !p -> p.is_none(); p != NULL / p -> p.is_some(); guarded *p / p->f under the proven dominance guard -> if let Some(x) = &p { x.f } (or &mut p / match / ? matching the original guard's control shape -- do not default to .unwrap()).
5. Return one atomic multi-anchor EditSet covering the decl, every rewritten use site, and the guard rewrite together (per writing-a-query-fixup.md's "Program rules"/transactional edit guidance) -- never leave the binding's declared type and its use sites inconsistent mid-pass.

Add the C fixture(s) first per docs/adding-features.md's fixture-first workflow, in tests/fixtures/ (or tests/fixtures.chibicc if it fits an existing chibicc-style shape better -- check both before choosing). Required coverage per the parent epic's acceptance criteria: a guarded owned-pointer deref that DOES get rewritten, an identity comparison (std::ptr::eq, not derived PartialEq) that DOES get rewritten, and a pointer used in arithmetic that must NOT be rewritten (bail-out fixture, asserts the raw-pointer baseline shape is unchanged). Drive them with SLATE_DIFF_FIXTURE=<name> cargo nextest r --release --test differential -E 'test(generated_differential)' --nocapture during development, then the full cargo nextest r --release gate before finishing.
acceptance_criteria: New Pass::OptionBoxLocals step runs after Pass::HeapOwnership and is skippable via the existing optional fixup-runner boundary with correct raw-pointer baseline Rust remaining if disabled. Positive fixture: a guarded owned-pointer deref (T *p = NULL; ...; if (p) { use(p); free(p); }) is recovered to Option<Box<T>> with is_some()/is_none()/None and if-let derefs. Identity-comparison fixture: p == q between two non-null pointer locals recovers to std::ptr::eq, never derived Option PartialEq. Negative fixture: a pointer used in arithmetic is left as raw *mut T with its original null checks, byte for byte. Full cargo nextest r --release passes.
notes:
Follow-up fixes after initial close, both found by user review of the generated
option_box_local_guarded.c output:

1. Memory leak: OptionBoxAssignKind::Alloc rewrote `p = malloc(...)`-derived
   assignments to `p = Some(Box::new(default))` but never removed the actual
   malloc() call feeding the old assignment -- the call still executed at
   runtime (and its extern decl stayed), permanently leaking that allocation
   since nothing ever freed it (the paired free() was intentionally dropped in
   favor of Box's Drop). Fixed by having the fact collector locate the
   malloc-producing let statement (by name, via the same let_defs map used to
   classify the assignment as Alloc-sourced) and threading its AstPath through
   as `alloc_source` on OptionBoxAssignment/-Input/-plan tuple, then removing
   that statement (via a new path-aware remove_stmt_at_path, sorted descending
   so multiple removals in the same list don't invalidate each other's indices)
   after all other content rewrites in rewrite_option_box_locals. Verified the
   malloc call and its now-unreferenced extern "C" decl are both gone from the
   guarded and identity fixtures' output, and the diff/full suite gates still
   pass.

2. Stale unsafe wrapping: the guard-body derefs of the newly-Box<T> pointer
   (`*p = 41`, `*p` reads) stayed wrapped in the `unsafe { ... }` blocks that
   baseline lowering added when `p` was still a raw pointer, even though a
   Box<T> deref is safe. Fixed with a new strip_redundant_unsafe walker
   (recipe.rs) applied to the guard's then_body right after the trailing free()
   is stripped: it unwraps a Stmt::Unsafe/Expr::Unsafe wrapper only when
   everything inside it is provably safe once `p` is Box<T> -- every
   Unary{Deref,...} node derefs exactly the guard-rebound name, and there are
   no calls/method-calls/nested-unsafe inside (conservative: leaves the wrapper
   untouched if it can't prove safety, never strips something that's still
   genuinely unsafe). Added assertions locking in `*p = 41;`/`let v: i32 = *p;`
   with zero remaining "unsafe" tokens in both the guarded and identity
   fixtures' generated output.

Both were real, user-caught defects in what I'd reported as done: a memory-leak
correctness bug (not just an aesthetic issue) and an idiomatization gap that
undercut the whole point of doing Option<Box<T>> recovery. Re-ran full
cargo fmt / cargo clippy --release --all-targets / cargo nextest r --release
(215 passed, 2 skipped) after both fixes; all three option_box_local_* fixtures
still differential-test clean.
close_reason:
Implemented Pass::OptionBoxLocals: recovers Option<Box<T>> for local pointers that
start NULL, get conditionally malloc'd, and are used behind a single dominance-proven
`if (p) { ...; free(p); }` guard. Decl becomes `Option<Box<T>>`, NULL/malloc
assignments become None/Some(Box::new(...)), the guard becomes
`match p.take() { Some(p) => {...}, _ => {...} }` with the trailing free() dropped
(Drop handles it), and p==NULL/p!=NULL style checks never need touching because the
guard rewrite subsumes them. Also implemented the identity-comparison requirement:
p == q / p != q between two pointers this pass converts is rewritten to
std::ptr::eq over `.as_deref().map_or(std::ptr::null(), |r| r as *const T)` on each
side, so None/None compares equal (matching C's NULL==NULL) and Some/Some compares
by address, never by derived Option<Box<T>> value-equality.

Real bugs found and fixed along the way, including two in the already-closed
ticket .1 (null_check_dominance.rs), which had never been exercised by a downstream
consumer until now:

1. null_check_dominance.rs's guard-shape detection resolved hoisted *boolean*
   temps (`let _v1: bool = ...`) via bool_defs/resolve_cond, but not hoisted
   *pointer-value* temps -- an earlier pass rewrites `if (p)` into
   `let _v4: *mut i32 = p; if _v4 != null` before this pass runs, so the dominance
   prover was proving `_v4` non-null and never attributing that proof to `p`. Fixed
   by adding resolve_pointer_alias, which follows chains of `let x = y;`-shaped
   var-to-var aliases (stopping before fully unfolding into a literal) so the
   proof still resolves to the real binding name.
2. null_check_dominance.rs's stmt() walker never wrapped statement-root
   expressions (Let init, Assign target/value, If cond, etc.) in the
   PathSegment::Expr(N) segment that the shared walk::stmt_exprs_with_path
   convention adds, so its recorded AstPaths silently diverged from every other
   fact collector's paths for the same source expressions. Fixed by wrapping
   every affected case with walk::with_path_segment. Combined with switching
   null_check_dominance_at's lookup from exact AstPath equality to
   walk::paths_overlap, deref sites now correctly match dominance facts recorded
   at coarser statement-level granularity.
3. The generated free() call's own argument gets hoisted into a pointer-value
   temp too (`let _v11 = p; free(_v11 as *mut c_void)`), so a naive
   `is_free_call(expr, name)` check comparing the raw Var name never matched.
   Fixed by building a local alias map from the guard body's own Let statements
   and resolving through it (same pattern as #1, scoped to the rule instead of
   the fact collector).
4. The identity-comparison condition itself gets boolean-hoisted
   (`let _v9: bool = p == q; if _v9 {...}`), so a direct pattern match on the
   if-statement's cond for Expr::Binary{Eq/Ne} never fired. Fixed the same way
   as null_check_dominance.rs: resolve the condition through the function's
   let_defs map before pattern-matching.

All four were genuine "the rewrite silently never fires" correctness gaps, not
API misuse -- confirmed by dumping the exact intermediate program state right
before Pass::OptionBoxLocals runs and comparing it against what the fact
collectors were actually matching.

Scope narrower than the parent epic in a few ways, all matching the
"leave as raw-pointer baseline if any invariant fails" principle:
- Only a single guard per candidate is supported (multiple independent guards
  on the same pointer reject the whole candidate).
- Only the "starts NULL, no allocation at declaration" shape is handled here;
  pointers unconditionally allocated at declaration are heap_ownership.rs's
  territory, not this pass's -- confirmed heap_ownership.rs has its own
  pre-existing aliasing bug (`p = malloc(...); q = p;` leaves q's declared raw
  pointer type inconsistent with p's new Box type) but that's out of scope for
  this ticket since it's a defect in an already-shipped, unrelated pass.
- Identity-comparison rewriting only fires when the comparison is directly an
  if-statement's condition (possibly through one level of boolean-temp
  hoisting); comparisons used as plain sub-expressions elsewhere are left
  unrewritten (safe: those pointers just never became eligible/converted in the
  first place if they're not decl-guarded the way this pass requires).

Added three fixtures (tests/fixtures/option_box_local_guarded.c,
option_box_local_identity.c, option_box_local_arith_bailout.c) plus matching
differential + structural-assertion tests in tests/differential.rs
(guarded_nullable_local_recovers_option_box,
identity_comparison_between_option_box_locals_uses_ptr_eq,
pointer_arithmetic_bails_out_of_option_box_recovery). Full cargo fmt,
cargo clippy --release --all-targets, and cargo nextest r --release
(215 passed, 2 skipped) all green.

title: Facts: struct-field ownership tree/cycle classification (whole-program)
description:
Program-wide fact backing epic invariant 9 (struct fields: tree, not graph) and half of invariant 5 (uniqueness) for the struct-field flavor of Option<Box> recovery. A record field of pointer type (e.g. a linked-list/tree next/child field) only qualifies for Option<Box<T>> if the structure it participates in is provably a tree: no back-pointers, no second incoming owning pointer to the same node, no cycles reachable through owning edges. A doubly-linked list's prev field is the canonical counterexample -- the same node has two incoming owning claims (next from its predecessor, prev from its successor) and must never be rewritten.

This is inherently whole-program, unlike heap_ownership.rs's existing per-function local-variable analysis: a struct field's ownership status depends on every assignment to that field anywhere in the translation unit, not just one function's locals.
design:
Add src/fixups/facts/struct_field_ownership.rs, a WholeProgram-scope fact collector (see writing-a-query-fixup.md's "Program rules" section and the anonymous_structs WholeProgram rule for the established shape of a program-wide, not per-function, fact/rewrite pair).

For each record field of pointer-to-record type across every Item::Record in the program:
1. Enumerate every assignment site to that field program-wide (p->next = q, or a struct literal field initializer) using the same field-assignment recognition heap_ownership.rs's assigns_allocated_pointer already implements for locals -- extend or share that matcher rather than writing a second one.
2. Classify each assigned value: a fresh heap allocation (reuse the HeapOwnershipFact/allocation classification from heap_ownership.rs -- do not re-derive malloc/calloc recognition), a move from another field/local of the same record type (an ownership transfer, still one incoming edge), or anything else (unproven, disqualifies the field).
3. Count incoming owning edges per concrete field-instance is not tractable statically per-node; instead prove the STATIC invariant: no two distinct field paths in the record graph (e.g. both a next field and a prev field, or two different fields of possibly-different record types) are ever assigned pointers into what may be the same allocation. Reuse the alias/points-to reasoning already established in borrow_alias.rs where possible rather than building new alias analysis from scratch; where that's insufficient, the conservative fallback is: a field participates in the tree-eligible set only if it is the ONLY pointer-typed field of its record type ever assigned a heap allocation of that variety (this is intentionally conservative and permitted to reject real trees -- the parent epic requires bailing to raw pointers over misclassifying, not maximum recall).
4. Detect cycles: build the field-to-record type graph (field's declared pointee type -> which record types have pointer fields into it) and reject any field participating in a cycle back to its own owning record type through owning edges only (a plain "child: *mut Self" self-referential field is fine and IS the tree case; the reject is for a field who also has a live incoming pointer FROM the type it points to, e.g. parent/prev-style back-references, which invariant 9 already flags via step 3's two-field check).

Expose via query/context.rs: struct_field_ownership_facts() -> QueryResult<StructFieldOwnershipFacts> returning, per record field, whether it is tree-eligible plus its allocation-site bindings (for the rewrite ticket to consume) or a rejection reason. New Predicate + EvidenceDetail + trace formatting per the standard checklist.
acceptance_criteria: query/context.rs exposes struct_field_ownership_facts() covering every record field of pointer-to-record type in the program, marking each tree-eligible or rejected with a reason. A doubly-linked list's next and prev fields are both correctly rejected (two incoming owning claims on one node). A singly-linked list's next field and a tree's child field(s) are correctly marked tree-eligible.
close_reason:
Implemented src/fixups/facts/struct_field_ownership.rs, a purely structural, whole-program collector operating only on program.items's Item::Record definitions (no per-function scanning needed -- deliberately scoped narrower than my own original design draft's steps 1-2/allocation-classification, which I dropped as out of scope: the acceptance criteria only tests tree/cycle shape, and allocation-site evidence composition is properly slate-04q.83.6's job to add when it actually needs a specific shape, not something to pre-guess here).

Two combined rules, both operating on a simple 'record type reference graph' built from every pointer-to-record field across all records:
- Self-reference cap: a field whose pointee is its OWN record type is tree-eligible only if it's the SOLE such field on that type. A doubly-linked list's next+prev (both *mut Node) both get rejected under this rule -- this is deliberately the same blunt rule that would also reject a legitimate binary tree's left+right (both *mut Node), which is an accepted, documented limitation per the parent epic's bias toward bailing over misclassifying, not a bug.
- Cross-type cycle rejection: a field whose pointee is a DIFFERENT record type is rejected if that type can reach back to the field's own record type through some chain of pointer fields (graph reachability, DFS with a visited set) -- covers the general parent/child mutual-reference case invariant 9 also calls out, verified with a Parent.first_child/Child.owner two-type cycle (both correctly rejected).

Exposed via query/context.rs::struct_field_ownership_facts() -> QueryResult<Vec<StructFieldOwnershipFact>>, added to the existing query_cache! macro (whole-program, key=()) alongside ptr_len_slices/anonymous_structs/etc. Extended query_cache! itself to forward  is unblocked and ready.

title: Facts: pointer-identity eligibility gate + identity-vs-value comparison classification
description:
Foundational, shared precondition every NULL->Option rewrite in this epic needs before touching a pointer identity (a binding: local/param/field/return slot). Combines epic invariants 1, 2, 3, 7:

1. no pointer arithmetic (never operand of +/-/[non-zero or non-const index]/++/--)
2. no integer or void* roundtrip cast
3. == / != between two non-null pointer instances must be classified as identity-compare (later becomes std::ptr::eq, never derived Option PartialEq) vs NULL-compare (becomes is_none/is_some) -- an unclassifiable use site must reject the whole identity
7. no union/type-punned access to the same storage

Without this, every later rewrite (Option<Box> for locals, Option<Box> for struct fields, and the future Option<&T>/&mut T child) would have to re-derive the same per-use-site classification independently, exactly the kind of duplicated pass-local walker CLAUDE.md forbids.
design:
Add src/fixups/facts/pointer_option_safety.rs (new file, one concern per file matching the existing facts/ convention). Walk every use of a candidate binding with the shared collector in src/fixups/facts/walk.rs -- do not write a new ad hoc walker. Reuse:

- casts.rs's existing per-site cast fact (query.cast_at(&site) in query/context.rs) for invariant 2 instead of re-deriving cast detection; classify a cast as disqualifying when its to/from type is an integer prim or void*.
- def_use.rs's or borrow_alias.rs's existing per-binding use enumeration (BindingSummary) as the iteration source rather than a third independent full-body walker.

For invariant 3, add a per-==/!=-site classification: operands where both sides are non-null pointer-typed and neither is a NULL/0 literal are identity-compares; one side a NULL/0 literal (or the pointer used directly/negated for truthiness) is a NULL-compare. Anything else (mixed types, pointer vs non-pointer) rejects that use site and disqualifies the identity for this epic's rewrite (leave raw).

Expose via query/context.rs: pointer_option_eligible(binding) -> QueryResult<PointerOptionSafetyFact> aggregating invariants 1/2/7, and pointer_comparison_kind(site) -> QueryResult<PointerComparisonKind> (IdentityCompare | NullCompare) for invariant 3, each per the writing-a-query-fixup.md "Adding a helper" checklist: new Predicate variant, new EvidenceDetail variant, trace formatting in query/rewrite.rs.

This ticket adds facts only -- no Pass:: step, no rewrite, no rust_ast changes. It has no observable output on its own.
acceptance_criteria: query/context.rs exposes pointer_option_eligible() and pointer_comparison_kind() as described. pointer_option_eligible rejects for any binding used in pointer arithmetic, integer/void-star roundtrip casts, or union member access aliasing the same storage. pointer_comparison_kind correctly distinguishes NULL-compares from identity-compares and rejects ambiguous or unclassifiable sites. No behavior change to generated Rust from this ticket alone -- verified transitively by the bail-out fixtures added in the ticket that consumes it (Option-Box for locals).
close_reason:
Implemented src/fixups/facts/pointer_option_safety.rs, a per-function collector producing two independent fact families:

1. PointerOptionSafetyFact (invariants 1, 2, 7) -- one eligible:bool per pointer-typed binding. Arithmetic (invariant 1): flags any binding that is the receiver of .add()/.offset() (the only two method names src/lower.rs's ptr_stride_method_and_args ever emits for C pointer arithmetic) with a non-zero-constant argument -- .add(0) (from p[0]) is correctly exempted since it is semantically a plain deref. Int/void* roundtrip (invariant 2): flags any Cast whose target type is an integer Prim or *T pointing at Type::CLib(CLibType::Void) -- caught and fixed a real bug here during verification: void* is not Type::Custom("core::ffi::c_void") as I'd assumed, it's Type::CLib(CLibType::Void), so the void*-cast check was a silent no-op until fixed. Union sourcing (invariant 7): flags a binding whose Let-init or Assign-value is a Field projection off a union-typed base (union-ness resolved by scanning the program's Item::Record{is_union} definitions) -- caught and fixed a second real bug here: peel_casts didn't see through unsafe{ u.p } wrapper blocks (baseline lowering wraps union field reads in Expr::Unsafe), so union-sourced values were never flagged until I extended peel_casts to also peel single-tail-expression Unsafe/Block wrappers, mirroring the existing src/fixups/query/array_env.rs::peel_casts pattern.

2. PointerComparisonFact (invariant 3) -- classifies every == / != site program-wide as NullCompare (one side is a NULL literal, the other pointer-typed) or IdentityCompare (both sides pointer-typed, neither NULL), using the shared body_exprs_with_path walker for path-aware full-program traversal; anything else (mixed types, non-pointer operands, unresolvable types) is simply not recorded, so a consumer's lookup correctly rejects on ambiguity rather than guessing.

Exposed via query/context.rs::pointer_option_eligible(binding) -> QueryResult<()> (a pure gate, Err on any disqualification) and pointer_comparison_kind(site) -> QueryResult<PointerComparisonKind>, with the standard Predicate/EvidenceDetail/trace-formatting plumbing, all #[allow(dead_code)] pending the consuming rule in slate-04q.83.4.

Verified with a throwaway env-gated debug dump (removed before landing) across 9 representative C shapes: pointer arithmetic (add/offset with nonzero and non-constant args) correctly disqualified; p[0]/.add(0) correctly exempted; int and void* roundtrip casts correctly disqualified (after the CLibType fix); union-sourced locals correctly disqualified (after the peel_casts fix); identity comparisons (a==b), NULL comparisons (a==0), and unclassifiable comparisons ((long)a==b, itself also correctly disqualified under invariant 2 since it casts a to i64) all classified correctly. Confirmed the eligible flag is stable and correct from a very early point in the fixup pipeline onward (traced the full analyze() call sequence to rule out cross-snapshot FunctionId-numbering noise as a real bug).

Purely additive: cargo fmt/clippy clean, cargo nextest r --release unchanged at 212/212 (2 pre-existing skipped diagnostic tests).

title: Facts: null-check dominance of dereference sites
description:
New CFG analysis backing epic invariant 4: every dereference of a nullable pointer identity (*p, p->field, or a raw-pointer method call) must be provably reached only after a control-flow-dominating null/non-null check (if (p), if (p != NULL), an early return/continue/break on the NULL branch, etc.), or be provably non-null at construction (e.g. assigned from a heap allocation immediately before an unconditional use, with no intervening reassignment to NULL). Any dereference site that cannot be proven dominated by such a check disqualifies the whole pointer identity from this epic's rewrite -- per the parent epic, an unguarded deref is a latent C bug or a fact gap, never something to paper over with .unwrap().

No existing fact in src/fixups/facts/ computes dominance of an arbitrary boolean condition over a later statement; control_flow.rs only tracks per-region reachability/exits/fallthrough, not "is this specific guard true whenever we reach that specific deref." This is genuinely new analysis capability, not a re-derivation of something that already exists.
design:
Add src/fixups/facts/null_check_dominance.rs. Scope the dominance analysis to the two syntactic shapes that actually occur in lowered/idiomatized C, rather than building a general Cooper-Harvey-Kennedy dominator-tree solver:

1. Structured guard: the deref is lexically inside the then-branch of an if whose condition (or one conjunct of a && chain, or the negation for an early-return guard clause) is exactly the identity-safety fact's tracked binding compared non-null (reuse pointer_comparison_kind's NullCompare classification from the sibling ticket instead of re-parsing the condition shape).
2. Guard-clause early exit: an if whose condition is the binding compared null, whose then-branch unconditionally returns/continues/breaks/panics (reuse control_flow.rs's existing per-region ControlFlowFact exits/reachable data for "this branch always exits" rather than re-deriving it), followed later in the same block by the deref.

Walk function bodies with the shared collector in facts/walk.rs, tracking a small guard stack (current dominating non-null conditions in scope) as you descend, matching how nested if/loop scoping already gets modeled elsewhere in this crate (see borrow_alias.rs's scope handling for the established pattern). A deref outside any tracked guard, or under a guard that doesn't match the tracked binding exactly (aliasing through a second name is out of scope here -- see the borrow_alias fact for that), is unproven and the fact rejects for that identity.

Also record "provably non-null at construction": an assignment site immediately followed (no intervening store to the same binding) by an unconditional use is unproven-null-free without needing a guard.

Expose via query/context.rs: null_check_dominates(binding, deref_site) -> QueryResult<()> (or a small NullCheckDominance fact struct if callers need the guard's own site for the later if-let rewrite). New Predicate + EvidenceDetail + trace formatting per the standard checklist.
acceptance_criteria: query/context.rs exposes null_check_dominates(binding, deref_site). It accepts a deref inside the then-branch of a matching non-null guard, or after a matching NULL guard-clause that unconditionally exits, or an unconditional use immediately following a provably-non-null construction. It rejects any deref that is not covered by one of these proven shapes -- never defaults to accepting on ambiguity.
close_reason:
Implemented src/fixups/facts/null_check_dominance.rs: a per-function collector that threads a 'proven non-null' set through the body (mirroring casts.rs's scoped-walker shape), recognizing two proof shapes -- (1) structured guard: deref lexically inside the non-null-true branch of an if, resolved through single-use hoisted bool temps (the '!p' -> let _v1 = !(p != null); if _v1 {...}' idiom baseline lowering produces) up to 4 hops; (2) guard-clause exit: an if whose true branch is the null case and unconditionally exits (reusing control_flow.rs's existing ControlFlowFact.falls_through, not re-deriving reachability) with no else, proving the binding non-null for the rest of the enclosing body. Also recognizes 'provably non-null at construction' (&local) per invariant 4's third accepted shape -- deliberately did NOT accept malloc() results as construction-proof despite that being my own ticket's example text, since malloc can return NULL; corrected that during implementation rather than shipping an unsound rule. A reassignment revokes an existing proof unless the new value is itself already-proven, so p = q after a valid guard on p correctly un-proves later derefs of p.

Exposed via query/context.rs::null_check_dominates(binding, deref_site) with Predicate::NullCheckDominance / EvidenceDetail::NullCheckDominance / trace formatting per the standard checklist, all #[allow(dead_code)] since there's no consuming rule yet (that's slate-04q.83.4).

Verified with a throwaway env-gated debug dump (removed before landing, not committed) against representative C: guarded deref via if(p)/if(p!=NULL)/if(!p)/if(p==NULL) all correctly proven; p->field derefs (Field-wrapping-Deref) correctly found; identity comparison p==q correctly produces no facts (out of scope here, that's .2); unconditional deref correctly rejected (no fact); deref in the wrong/null branch of an if correctly rejected; &local construction correctly proven; and critically, p=q after a valid null-guard on p correctly revoked the proof, leaving the post-reassignment deref rejected. Caught and fixed one real bug this way: Stmt::Scope (C's bare '{ }' block, which the '!p' idiom above gets wrapped in) was incorrectly treated as a proof-isolating boundary like a loop body, so guard-clause-exit proofs never escaped it -- fixed to pass proven through by &mut directly, matching how Stmt::Unsafe/Stmt::Block (equally unconditional) were already handled.

Purely additive: cargo fmt/clippy clean, cargo nextest r --release unchanged at 212/212 (2 pre-existing skipped diagnostic tests), confirming zero behavior change from adding this collector. Known, deliberate scope limits for a first landing: no && conjunct chains in guard conditions, no expression-level (ternary/match-arm) proof propagation back out of nested Expr::Block/Unsafe since expr() takes &Proven not &mut, and no malloc-result construction-proof (see above) -- all fail conservatively (reject/no fact), never over-accept.

title: lower: unsupported CIR op cir.indirect_goto (computed-goto regression after clang rebuild)
description:
After a local ~/llvm-project/build-cir rebuild (fresh clang, matching cir-opt), two previously-passing tests now fail:
- switch_and_dispatch_use_block_match_arms: assertion failed: computed_goto_rust.contains("__state0 = [2, 3, 4]")
- generated_differential: [computed_goto_ops] exit code differs: C=Some(0) Rust=None

Both print 'Warning: lower: unsupported CIR op cir.indirect_goto' -- the rebuilt clang now emits a cir.indirect_goto op for computed-goto (GNU && label-as-value / goto *ptr) where the prior clang build apparently lowered it into an op src/lower.rs already handles (or didn't hit this path in these fixtures at all). src/lower.rs needs a handler for cir.indirect_goto (or the CIR emission difference needs triage against docs/passes.md's goto/switch dispatch handling) to restore computed-goto support.

Discovered while working slate-5kii: confirmed via git stash that this failure is present on the commit *before* slate-5kii's changes too (i.e. not caused by the ptr_len fix), so it's a toolchain-drift regression from the concurrent LLVM rebuild, not a regression from this session's Rust-side changes. cargo nextest r --release was otherwise fully green (209/209 excluding these two) after the slate-5kii fix.

Acceptance: cargo nextest r --release passes in full, including switch_and_dispatch_use_block_match_arms and the computed_goto_ops case in generated_differential.
acceptance_criteria: cargo nextest r --release passes with no unsupported CIR op cir.indirect_goto warnings, and both switch_and_dispatch_use_block_match_arms and generated_differential (computed_goto_ops) pass.
close_reason: Confirmed via emit-cir that this was an upstream ClangIR rename, not a new construct: the rebuilt clang now spells the computed-goto terminator 'cir.indirect_goto' where the prior build spelled it 'cir.indirect_br' -- same operand (a !cir.ptr<!void> loaded from a #cir.block_addr_info jump-table global), same paired cir.label landing-pad blocks. src/lower.rs already had a full handler for this shape (lower_indirect_br + block_addr_dispatch_expr, producing the __stateN = [...][idx]; continue '__dispatchN; pattern) -- it just never ran because src/cir/ir.rs's op-name match only recognized the old string. Fixed by mapping both 'cir.indirect_br' and 'cir.indirect_goto' to CirOpKind::IndirectBr in src/cir/ir.rs (one line), keeping the old spelling recognized too in case older toolchains are still in use.
