title: Define memchr query semantics and expand differential coverage
description:
Why: memchr is the first query-engine migration and needs an explicit behavioral oracle before infrastructure changes obscure semantic regressions. The current zero-needle optimization uses a known NUL position without proving that the searched count includes it.

Scope:
- Expand the focused C differential fixture for full-buffer hits and misses, zero-length searches, and NUL searches where count is greater than, equal to, or less than the first NUL index.
- Cover unknown or partial counts, unsupported source provenance, const/mutable pointer views, and a nonconstant but pure needle where practical.
- State the exact proof obligations for the optimized NUL case and the general byte-position case.
- Correct the legacy behavior narrowly if required to keep the new semantic oracle green before the query migration lands.
- Preserve conservative fallback whenever the searched byte range cannot be proven safe.
design: The NUL optimization is legal only when the first NUL index is known and first_nul < count. The general iterator-position rewrite initially requires a proven readable byte view whose extent equals the memchr count. Argument evaluation must remain observable exactly once; fixture cases should expose dropped, duplicated, or delayed evaluation where relevant. This task establishes behavior and output expectations but does not build the query engine.
acceptance_criteria:
- Focused C fixture coverage distinguishes count > first_nul, count == first_nul, and count < first_nul.
- Complete-buffer hit/miss, zero count, unknown/partial count, and unsupported provenance remain differentially correct.
- Output-shape assertions identify which cases rewrite and which remain on the conservative helper path.
- The proof obligations consumed by the future query rules are recorded in the bead notes or relevant design documentation.
- cargo fmt, cargo clippy, and cargo nextest r --release pass.
notes:
Implemented semantic oracle and legacy guard.

Proof obligations for the future query rules:
- Candidate must be the generated __slate_memchr call with exactly source, needle, and count arguments.
- Source must resolve to a supported byte view with binding/type provenance and pointer mutability.
- Known-NUL shortcut requires a well-formed existing string-buffer fact, a known first-NUL index, needle proven equal to zero, and first_nul < count. Equality does not include the terminator. Missing count/range evidence leaves the helper call unchanged.
- General iter().position() rewrite initially requires count proven equal to the complete readable byte extent. Partial/unknown extents and unsupported offset-pointer provenance leave the helper call unchanged.
- Any query migration must preserve evaluation count/order: arguments moved into closures or omitted by the recipe require purity/stability evidence or explicit materialization.

Coverage added in tests/fixtures/mem_memchr.c: runtime-derived pure needle, full-extent mutable and const sources, full hit/miss, zero count, NUL count greater/equal/less than first NUL, volatile runtime partial count, and offset-pointer unsupported provenance.

Validation: cargo fmt --check; cargo clippy; cargo nextest r --release (201 passed, 2 skipped).
close_reason: Completed memchr semantic oracle, corrected NUL range proof, and passed all quality gates.

title: Make fixups query-driven and migrate rewrite passes
description:
Why: Slate rewrite passes currently mix AST traversal, local shape matching, fact lookup, proof gating, mutation, scheduling, and tracing. This makes each rewrite larger and harder to audit than the semantic rule it implements. Introduce a query-driven rewrite layer whose rule-authoring interface makes preconditions, captures, and the desired typed AST transformation concise, while allowing the engine and fact adapter to carry the implementation complexity.

Scope:
- Add src/fixups/query/ as the shared query and rewrite-engine implementation.
- Adapt Program plus each facts::analyze snapshot into an indexed query context; existing fact collectors remain the semantic source of truth during migration.
- Centralize node selection/traversal so rules query matching AST nodes and facts instead of implementing pass-local walkers.
- Let rules state positive proof requirements, local versus function/program scope, captures, fallback/specificity, and a typed transformation recipe. The interface need not resemble SQL, Datalog, or another data language; ergonomics and auditability of individual rules are the primary requirement.
- Apply query results deterministically to structured Rust AST nodes, detect conflicting or overlapping edits, and preserve the no-rendered-string-rewrites invariant.
- After a changed query round/pass, analyze the updated AST again before later rules that require fresh facts, preserving the current correctness model while moving scheduling behind the engine.
- Support incremental coexistence with legacy rewrites, then migrate every rewrite pass piece by piece.
- Use memchr_prelude::fixup_calls as the first end-to-end migration, covering its specific NUL-search optimization, general byte-position fallback, and unchanged fallback when proof is insufficient.
- Integrate accepted/rejected rule decisions and consumed facts with fixup tracing; coordinate focused fact provenance/debug behavior with slate-idu.

Out of scope for the first slice: designing a standalone textual query language, migrating every pass at once, incremental fact invalidation, or moving correctness from baseline lowering into fixups.
design:
Create a small rule-authoring surface over a more capable private engine. A rule should identify a node kind/semantic operation, bind arguments and relevant entities, list proof predicates over AST shape and FixupFacts, and return a typed rewrite recipe or no match. Recipes construct rust_ast Expr/Stmt/Item values and may produce expression-local, region, function-signature, or program plans; rendered source is never an input or output of matching.

The query context is built from a Program and immutable FixupFacts snapshot and provides indexed access by FunctionId, BindingId, call identity, and AstPath. Missing evidence is unknown and cannot authorize a rewrite. Universal claims such as all uses or all callers require an explicit complete domain and at least one member, so indirect/escaped/external references stay conservative.

The engine collects intents against one snapshot, rejects ambiguous overlapping intents unless specificity/priority resolves an intentional fallback, applies a deterministic non-overlapping batch, and reports whether the AST changed. Scheduling then invokes facts::analyze on the changed Program before the next fact-dependent round/pass. Start with whole-snapshot recomputation rather than incremental invalidation.

During migration, query-backed and legacy passes share the existing pass ordering and trace identities. The memchr migration establishes the vertical slice: AST/call lookup, value and string/buffer fact predicates, ordered specific/general alternatives, typed Expr construction, trace provenance, reanalysis, differential behavior, and unchanged fallback. Later child work migrates passes by semantic cluster until pass-local matching/walking boilerplate can be removed.
acceptance_criteria:
- src/fixups/query/ exists and exposes a documented, typed rule interface centered on declarative preconditions/captures plus a transformation recipe; a typical call rewrite does not implement its own recursive AST walker or manually join raw fact vectors.
- Program and FixupFacts snapshots can be converted/indexed into the query context without changing collector semantics, and rules can query nodes, call identities, values, bindings, effects, and domain-completeness proofs needed by migrated passes.
- Query execution updates only structured rust_ast nodes, is deterministic, detects conflicting/overlapping edits, and emits rule-level trace evidence for applied and useful rejected candidates.
- A changed fact-dependent query round is followed by facts::analyze on the updated AST before the next dependent rule/pass; tests demonstrate that a later rule sees facts exposed by an earlier rewrite.
- memchr_prelude::fixup_calls is migrated first with behavioral and output-shape parity or improvement, including correct first-n-byte bounds for NUL search, byte-position fallback when proven safe, and no rewrite when evidence is insufficient.
- Legacy and query-backed passes coexist throughout migration with stable pass ordering and fixup-debug behavior.
- Every existing rewrite is represented by child migration work and the epic closes only after all rewrite passes use the query method where applicable, bespoke traversal/matching boilerplate has been removed, and docs/facts.md, docs/writing-a-fixup.md, and docs/passes.md describe the new workflow.
- cargo fmt, cargo clippy, and cargo nextest r --release pass for each implementation slice and as the final completion gate.
notes:
First implementation milestone: establish the query directory, snapshot adapter, minimal rule API, engine scheduling/reanalysis, and migrate memchr_prelude::fixup_calls. Create focused child beads before implementation.

Inventoried the C23 <threads.h> surface against cppreference and the active glibc header. Added one consolidated deterministic fixture at tests/stdlib/threads/functions.c covering all 25 mandatory functions: the eight thrd_* functions, six mtx_* functions, six cnd_* functions, four tss_* functions, and call_once. title: Investigate setjmp.h support
description: Inventory the C23 public interface of <setjmp.h> using cppreference and the active Clang/libc headers. Add deterministic C-only differential coverage under tests/stdlib/setjmp/ for every callable function and function-like macro exposed by the header, plus minimal probes for public types, object-like macros, and constants where relevant. Exercise each interface rather than relying on include-only compilation. For every probe Slate cannot translate, compile, link, run, or match, preserve a minimal reproduction in the appropriate fixture location and file a focused child bug describing the CIR, lowering, ABI, platform, or runtime gap. Do not omit an interface merely because it is currently unsupported. Reference: https://en.cppreference.com/c/header/setjmp
design:
Panic/catch_unwind structural lowering (chosen direction, see slate-nk3.19's
notes for the fuller rejected-alternatives writeup):

Recognize the libcheck/minicheck-style idiom: a single (global or
thread-local) jmp_buf, one call site where `if (setjmp(&buf) == 0) { body }
else { recovery }` (or the `rc = setjmp(&buf); if (rc == 0) {...} else
{...}` desugared form) installs the recovery point, and one or more
`longjmp(&buf, val)` call sites arbitrarily deep in the call graph that
unwind back to it. This is exactly Rust's panic/catch_unwind shape, and is
sound (unlike a raw FFI setjmp/longjmp call, which is UB per slate-zmoi --
rustc has no returns_twice mechanism, stable or nightly, since 1.78).

Rewrite:
  - setjmp call site -> std::panic::catch_unwind(AssertUnwindSafe(|| { body }));
    match on Ok(()) / Err(payload), downcast payload to recover the longjmp
    value for the recovery branch.
  - longjmp(&buf, val) -> std::panic::panic_any(val) (or a dedicated payload
    type to avoid downcast collisions with unrelated i32 panics elsewhere in
    the same crate).
  - Any extern "C" fn reachable (transitively) from a longjmp call site must
    become extern "C-unwind" fn (stable since 1.71, ABI-compatible with
    plain "C", differs only in unwind-across-boundary behavior) or the
    process aborts instead of unwinding when a panic tries to cross it.
    This matters concretely for C-ABI callback handlers (e.g. expat's
    XML_StartElementHandler-shaped functions) that can call fail()/assert
    macros internally. Scope via call-graph reachability from each
    longjmp site, or fall back to blanket "C-unwind" for all C-ABI-exported
    fns reachable from test/handler code if precise reachability is too
    costly.
  - Initial support restricted to a single statically-identifiable
    global/thread-local jmp_buf per recovery scope, non-nested, same-thread;
    reject ambiguous/escaping/nested setjmp uses (matches slate-nk3.19's
    scoping note).
  - Drop semantics improve over the original C (panic unwind correctly runs
    Rust Drop for locals in the unwound frames; longjmp skips all C cleanup
    by design) -- not a regression, and doesn't need special handling.

Concrete validation target: expat's tests/minicheck.c (a libcheck clone)
uses exactly this single-global-jmp_buf pattern for fail()/assert_true(),
transliterated to src/minicheck.rs's raw setjmp/longjmp FFI calls in
transpiled/libexpat. That raw-FFI version hangs (100% CPU, no progress)
partway through the real runtests suite -- reproducible, not a timing
fluke -- consistent with the known UB. After implementing the fixup pass,
retranslate libexpat with the corrected (XML_TESTING-flavored,
bear-captured) compile_commands.json, rebuild the runtests binary (already
wired up as a real [[bin]] target in transpiled/libexpat), and confirm the
full suite now runs to completion without hanging and matches the real C
runtests output (100%: Checks: 4836, Failed: 0).
acceptance_criteria: Every C23 interface in <setjmp.h> has deterministic e2e coverage or an explicit documented reason it cannot be exercised deterministically or on the configured platform; supported probes differentially match C; every failure has a focused child issue and minimal reproduction; required formatting, lint, and full release nextest gates pass for enabled fixtures.
notes: Implemented the chosen catch_unwind/panic_any structural lowering as Pass::SetjmpRecovery (src/fixups/query/rules/setjmp_recovery.rs), covering the single-global-jmp_buf if(setjmp(&buf)){recovery}body idiom from tests/fixtures/setjmp_recovery_guard.c (both a same-function guard and a guard whose longjmp fires from a callee, non-nested). Runs as the last fixup pass so every earlier idiom-recovery pass (printf_format, etc.) already sees flat pre-closure code -- wrapping statements in the catch_unwind closure makes them invisible to the shared support::walk-based statement-container walkers most other passes rely on. Rejects (leaves the raw FFI baseline untouched) on: a body with any return/break/continue other than a single trailing bare return; in the function's own top-level body, or a guard that's the last statement of a non-top-level container (would need to escape further up than this pass tracks). Payload is a dedicated per-buffer struct (__SlateJmpPayload_<buf>) via panic_any, with downcast-or-resume_unwind at each catch_unwind site, so an unrelated Rust panic (or a different buffer's payload) isn't silently swallowed at the wrong boundary. Discovered and fixed a real, separate blocker along the way: the test harness (tests/support/mod.rs) built every generated crate with panic="abort", which makes catch_unwind unconditionally unable to catch anything -- switched to panic="unwind" and relaxed compare_runs' exit-code check to treat a C process killed by a signal (e.g. abort()) as matching Rust's standard uncaught-panic exit code 101, preserving the existing abort-equivalence for fixtures like assert_recovery's recovered assert!() calls. Full release nextest (253/253) passes. Filed slate-nk3.35.1 for the extern "C-unwind" ABI propagation this doesn't yet cover (nothing exercises it). Broader scope remains open: the rest of setjmp.h's interface (sigsetjmp et al.), multi-buffer scoping, and tests/stdlib/setjmp/ coverage per this issue's acceptance criteria are untouched.

A diagnostic run with the long-double function calls omitted proved every float and double family plus complex construction and CMPLXL passes differential coverage. The complete fixture exposes one shared lowering failure: generated alloca frames initialize Complex<LongDouble> members with untyped integer zeros, so Rust compilation fails before long-double complex ABI behavior can be checked. Added shared run_once_program and run_once_items scheduling alongside the existing program and per-function fixpoint runners, plus a bounded fact-refreshing to_fixpoint_items_with_facts runner. Goto now implements Fixup and runs to whole-program function-item fixpoint. Switch implements Fixup and runs once. EarlyInlineTemps implements Fixup and runs to fixpoint with facts reanalyzed before every round while preserving the five-round large-program cap. AnonymousStructs remains an explicit program-wide exception and runs once through the program runner. ParamSpills stores facts/function/logger on its struct, remains an explicit FnDef-level exception because it mutates parameters, and runs once through the per-function runner. Removed obsolete NoopLogger wrappers and the unused early/late inline wrapper modules. Updated docs/writing-a-fixup.md for the runner architecture. Validation: cargo fmt; cargo check --release; cargo clippy --all-targets; cargo nextest r --release (176 passed, 2 skipped); git diff --check.

title: Unify body rewrite passes behind explicit Fixup runners
description:
Why: fixup orchestration in src/fixups/mod.rs obscures whether a rewrite runs once or to convergence. Most rewrite modules expose a thin module::fixup function that creates a NoopLogger-backed pass struct and immediately calls its method, while the production pipeline separately constructs the same struct and repeats item/function traversal and fixpoint loops. Facts-backed fixpoint passes also duplicate analyze-visit-repeat logic.

Refactor the body-oriented rewrite passes around one Fixup trait whose only method input is &mut Vec<IndentStmt> and whose boolean result reports whether that invocation changed the body. Each pass struct should own or borrow every other dependency it needs, including the logger, FunctionId, FixupFacts, pass phase, and configuration. Remove convergence loops from individual pass implementations so orchestration, not the pass, states whether it runs once or to a fixpoint.

Add explicit shared runners for run-once and to-fixpoint execution over function items. The call site in apply_with_logger must instantiate the concrete pass and select the runner, making convergence behavior obvious. Facts-backed passes must use the same runner model with an explicit fact-refresh policy that reanalyzes the program between fixpoint rounds when required. Prefer a parameter or small policy enum on the common runner family over a parallel helper if that remains clear and borrow-checker-friendly; otherwise use a clearly named to_fixpoint_items_with_facts helper.

Start from the existing Fixup implementations for struct_field_init and var_aliases. Audit body-oriented passes and migrate their thin module::fixup wrappers and hand-written loops. Program-wide or FnDef-shape rewrites that cannot honestly implement the body trait should remain explicit and be documented as exceptions rather than forced through a misleading adapter.
design:
Target shape:
- Fixup::fixup(&mut self, body: &mut Vec<IndentStmt>) -> bool performs one invocation/round.
- run_once_items makes a single pass over eligible function bodies.
- to_fixpoint_items repeats until a full program round reports no change.
- Facts-aware execution analyzes at the required boundary and constructs a pass with FunctionId plus FixupFacts already stored in the struct. For fixpoint passes that can invalidate facts, reanalyze before every round.
- apply_with_logger explicitly constructs each concrete pass and visibly chooses run_once_items or to_fixpoint_items plus the fact-refresh policy.
- Preserve special bounded convergence such as inline temp round limits through an explicit runner option or documented specialized runner.

Likely facts-refresh migrations include zero_init, dead_locals, call_args, final_return_temps, and atomic_compare_exchange. Plain body fixpoint migrations include struct_field_init, var_aliases, constant_conditions, ptr_copy, for_continue, singleton_scopes, and other eligible passes. Confirm the final list by auditing src/fixups/rewrite.
acceptance_criteria:
- Eligible body rewrite structs implement one common Fixup trait and take only &mut Vec<IndentStmt> in fixup; logger, facts, function identity, phase, and pass-specific configuration live on the struct.
- Thin module-level fixup wrappers that only create a NoopLogger and delegate are removed or replaced by direct pass construction in tests and production.
- Shared run_once_items and to_fixpoint_items runners exist, and every migrated call site explicitly selects one.
- Facts-backed runners support explicit reanalysis between fixpoint rounds; zero_init and every other facts-invalidating loop preserve current reanalysis behavior.
- A Fixup invocation performs one round; passes such as var_aliases do not hide their own completion loop beneath the shared fixpoint runner.
- Program-wide/FnDef-level passes that cannot use the body trait are audited and left as clear, documented exceptions.
- Pass ordering, skip/debug boundaries, rewrite logging, generated Rust, and differential behavior remain unchanged.
- cargo fmt, cargo clippy, and cargo nextest r --release pass; all test commands use nextest.
close_reason: Closed

title: Audit GNU libm and optional companion-library extensions

title: Emit portable libc runtime symbol signatures
description: The translated GNU libc string/stdio fixtures redeclare strlen as taking *mut i8 and returning u64. rustc flags this as a suspicious definition of a runtime symbol because the portable signature is const char pointer to usize. Output matches on x86_64, but the declaration is not target-portable.
acceptance_criteria: Known runtime symbols use target-correct C ABI types and qualifiers; the GNU libc fixtures compile without suspicious_runtime_symbol_definitions warnings on supported targets.

description: Configured Clang accepts __builtin_debugtrap, but Slate emits panic!("unsupported CIR op: cir.call_llvm_intrinsic") for it. The current completion fixture keeps the call on an untaken volatile branch so ordinary output can still be compared.

close_reason: Implemented Clang-resolved GCC visibility push/pop handling with nested stack export coverage and conservative conditional translate-directives rejection

gets removal is a negative C11 rule rather than an executable positive probe. Other optional __STDC_NO_* macros report atomics, complex, threads, and VLA frontend availability.

title: Support C17
description: Track the ISO C17 delta over C11. C17 introduces no new language syntax, headers, or library APIs: it updates __STDC_VERSION__ to 201710L, incorporates C11 defect resolutions, and deprecates ATOMIC_VAR_INIT plus zero-size realloc support. Cumulative language support continues to inherit the C11 epic; no separate feature-matrix fixture is required.
acceptance_criteria: The C17 delta is classified as having no new Slate feature surface; deprecations require no new lowering support; cumulative C17 support is represented by C11 support plus the frontend-provided __STDC_VERSION__ value and incorporated defect semantics.
notes: Closed as a no-new-feature delta. This closure does not claim unresolved C11/C99 features are supported; it records that C17 adds no separate feature-matrix work. C23 now directly depends on C11 so closing this bookkeeping epic does not incorrectly unblock the cumulative standards chain.
close_reason: C17 adds no new feature surface beyond C11; its only changes are the version macro, defect corrections, and deprecations that do not require a new Slate feature matrix.

cargo run -- translate succeeds with both the default frontend mode and SLATE_CLANG_ARGS=-std=c89.

title: Make the macro-dump plugin default worktree-independent
description:
Why: c_ast.rs currently defaults SLATE_MACRO_DUMP_PLUGIN to CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR/tools/macro-dump-plugin/build/MacroDump.so. That artifact is git-ignored and exists only in the checkout where it was built, so every ticket worktree fails the full test suite unless the environment variable is set manually.

What to do:
- Derive the default plugin path from the selected SLATE_CLANG build root, alongside the Clang toolchain rather than the Slate checkout.
- Update the plugin build script to install to that stable default path.
- Retain SLATE_MACRO_DUMP_PLUGIN as an explicit override.
- Update toolchain documentation and add path-resolution coverage.
acceptance_criteria: A plugin built once is found by main and all Git worktrees without setting SLATE_MACRO_DUMP_PLUGIN; custom absolute SLATE_CLANG paths derive the matching build-tree plugin path; the explicit plugin override still wins; documentation and build output agree on the default.
close_reason: Kept the git-ignored MacroDump.so build artifact in the Slate tree, installed an ABI-matched copy into the selected Clang build lib directory, and made c_ast default to that stable path while preserving SLATE_MACRO_DUMP_PLUGIN override. Verified from a separate worktree and on merged main with all 702 release nextest tests.

title: Lower #error to cfg-gated compile_error!
description:
Why: #error expresses an intentional compile-time rejection and currently either disappears in an inactive branch or prevents Clang AST/CIR extraction when active. Rust compile_error! is the direct semantic equivalent.

What to do:
- Add a typed Rust AST item for compile_error rather than Item::Raw text.
- Capture the unexpanded #error message using Clang-compatible whitespace handling.
- Inject an unconditional compile_error item for an active single configuration.
- Under translate-directives, wrap conditional errors in Item::Cfg using the effective recovered predicate.
- Refuse translation when a conditional error cannot be mapped faithfully instead of making it unconditional.
- Add output and compile-failure tests for unconditional, active, inactive, nested, and escaped-message cases.
acceptance_criteria: Unconditional and representable conditional #error directives produce typed compile_error items with correct messages; selected Rust configurations fail compilation exactly where the corresponding C configurations do; unmappable conditional errors produce a translation diagnostic; no Item::Raw bridge is used.
close_reason: Lowered #error through generic typed item macros, preserved source messages, cfg-gated conditional errors, refused unmappable predicates, and added directive E2E compile checks.

title: Define directive dispositions and correctness-preserving fallback
description:
Why: progressively supporting directives requires one exhaustive policy so unknown semantic effects are not silently discarded and diagnostic-only or Clang-consumed directives are not needlessly rejected.

What to do:
- Add a typed disposition for directives represented in Rust, consumed by Clang, diagnostic-only, no-output, and unsupported-semantic.
- Diagnose unknown and unsupported active directives with source context.
- Emit cfg-gated compile_error only when the enclosing condition is representable; otherwise stop translation.
- Never use TODO comments or runtime todo! as a correctness fallback.
- Make the classification exhaustive so adding a directive kind requires an explicit policy.
acceptance_criteria: Every recorded directive has an explicit disposition; unsupported semantic directives cannot silently yield buildable Rust; diagnostics identify directive spelling and location; inactive or cfg-gated cases fail only in configurations where their condition applies.
close_reason: Added exhaustive typed directive names and dispositions, enforced active unsupported-directive rejection across single-file and project translation, emitted cfg-gated compile_error fallbacks for representable conditional cases, and verified ledger/source-context behavior with E2E tests.

title: Provide location-preserving sanitized Clang input for directives
description:
Why: active fatal directives such as #error make Clang exit before Slate can obtain AST and CIR, but deleting or moving source changes offsets, include lookup, __FILE__, and source-location joins.

What to do:
- Build a Clang-only sanitized source representation from directive ledger spans.
- Replace selected directive bytes with whitespace while preserving byte length and newlines.
- Present the sanitized content under the original virtual path so relative includes, __FILE__, macro offsets, AST locations, and CIR locations remain stable.
- Use the same representation for CIR emission and Clang AST plus macro-plugin collection.
- Add tests proving locations and includes remain unchanged.
acceptance_criteria: Slate can run both Clang frontend paths after sanitizing a fatal directive; original path, line, and byte-offset joins remain valid; relative includes and __FILE__ behavior do not change; unsanitized translation behavior is unchanged.
close_reason: Added location-preserving Clang VFS overlays for selected directive spans and used one overlay for CIR, AST, and macro-plugin collection. Added CLI E2E coverage proving fatal logical directives no longer block frontends while relative includes, __FILE__, macro offsets, and cfg item locations remain stable. Verified cargo fmt, cargo clippy, 36 directive E2E tests, and all 703 release tests before merge.

title: Rename translate-cfg to translate-directives
description:
Why: the command will recover preprocessing directives beyond cfg conditionals, so translate-cfg is now the wrong public and internal name.

What to do:
- Rename the CLI command to translate-directives.
- Rename the cfg_translate module and relevant functions, test files, fixture documentation, and user-facing references.
- Preserve the current generated Rust semantics and command behavior under the new name.
- Decide explicitly whether translate-cfg is removed or retained only as a documented compatibility alias; do not maintain two independent implementations.
acceptance_criteria: Help and documentation present translate-directives as the public command; existing cfg translation coverage runs through the renamed implementation with unchanged output semantics; no stale internal cfg_translate naming remains except any deliberate compatibility alias.
close_reason: Renamed the public CLI, internal module/function, integration target, diagnostics, paths, and docs from translate-cfg/cfg_translate to translate-directives/directive_translate; removed the old command without an alias. Verified cargo fmt, cargo clippy, and all 702 release nextest tests on merged main.

title: Build a source-level preprocessing directive ledger
description:
Why: the current preprocessing oracle only recognizes six conditional directives one physical line at a time. General directive recovery needs a structured source record that also covers inactive regions and preserves exact source positions.

What to do:
- Parse preprocessing logical lines, including backslash-newline continuation and directive-leading whitespace.
- Record directive kind, raw payload, byte and line spans, nesting depth, effective enclosing predicate, and active state.
- Preserve the existing conditional-chain and predicate behavior while making it consume the ledger.
- Add focused tests for nested conditions, inactive directives, continuations, comments, and malformed nesting.
acceptance_criteria: The ledger records active and inactive directives with stable source spans and effective conditions; existing record-cfg and translate-cfg conditional tests remain green; logical-line and nesting cases are covered.
close_reason: Implemented a raw-source directive ledger with logical-line splicing, source spans, nesting depth, effective predicates, three-valued activity, comment-aware scanning, record-cfg JSON exposure, and focused unit/integration coverage. Verified cargo fmt, cargo clippy, and 702 release nextest tests on merged main.

title: Generalize translate-cfg into translate-directives
description:
Why: translate-cfg already reads raw C source and reconstructs conditional preprocessing structure, but its name and model are artificially limited to cfg recovery. Slate needs a source-level directive pipeline that can progressively preserve common directives such as #error while retaining explicit failure for unsupported semantic directives. Macro expansion recovery is a separate concern handled by the out-of-tree Clang macro-dump plugin and its AST/CIR joins.

Scope:
- Rename the translate-cfg command and implementation surface to translate-directives, updating help, tests, fixtures, and documentation.
- Preserve all existing conditional-to-Rust-cfg behavior and output under the renamed command.
- Replace the conditional-only line scanner with a directive ledger over preprocessing logical lines, recording kind, payload, byte/line span, enclosing conditional predicate, active state, and disposition.
- Extend directive support incrementally, beginning with #error lowered to a typed Rust AST compile_error item, conditionally wrapped in Item::Cfg when applicable.
- Classify common directives into: represented directly in Rust, consumed semantically by Clang, diagnostic-only, no-output, or unsupported-semantic.
- Add explicit handling plans for #warning, #define/#undef, includes/imports, #line, common pragmas, #embed, #ident/#sccs, and null directives.
- Provide a correctness-preserving fallback: unsupported active semantic directives stop translation or emit a cfg-gated compile_error; they are never silently dropped, emitted as a TODO comment, or deferred to runtime with todo!().

Out of scope:
- General reconstruction of C macro definitions or invocations. Active macro provenance remains the responsibility of tools/macro-dump-plugin and recognized AST/CIR recovery paths.
- Guessing mappings for predicates or directives whose semantics cannot be represented faithfully.
design: Raw source is authoritative for directive spelling, inactive branches, logical-line spans, and conditional nesting. Clang preprocessing callbacks may enrich or cross-check the active configuration, while macro expansion events remain a separate stream. Directive events do not require corresponding AST or CIR nodes; lowering injects typed Rust AST items where needed. Fatal source diagnostics such as #error require a Clang-only sanitized input that preserves the original virtual path, byte offsets, and newlines, followed by injection of compile_error into the generated Program. If an enclosing condition maps to Rust cfg, wrap the item in Item::Cfg; if it cannot be mapped portably, fail translation rather than make the error unconditional. Directives already reflected in Clang AST/CIR are recorded as consumed and are not reconstructed unless additional Rust syntax is required.
acceptance_criteria: The public command is named translate-directives and all prior translate-cfg integration coverage passes through it with unchanged generated Rust semantics. Raw-source directive records include logical spans and effective enclosing conditions for both active and inactive regions. Unconditional and cfg-gated #error directives generate typed compile_error items while Clang AST/CIR extraction still succeeds from a location-preserving sanitized input. Common directive families have documented dispositions and tests. Unsupported semantic directives cannot silently produce buildable Rust: translation fails or generated Rust contains an appropriately gated compile_error. Macro expansion recovery remains separate and existing recognized macro-constant behavior is unchanged. cargo fmt, cargo clippy, and cargo nextest r --release pass.
close_reason: All child tickets closed: .5-.9 (directive dispositions/fallback/pragma engineering), .10 (STDC FP pragmas, superseded by slate-0ar5's FenvAttr shim work), .11 (#pragma pack layout, verified structurally sound via Clang's MaxFieldAlignmentAttr), .12 (vendor pragma audit, found and fixed a real unroll/clang-optimize/clang-loop/clang-attribute/clang-fp-contract classification gap). translate-directives now has a documented pragma disposition table (docs/src/translate-directives.md) and no known silent-miscompile gaps in the audited pragma surface.

title: Lower Clang __float128 to native Rust f128
description: Why: Slate recognizes CIR float, double, and long double but had no representation for IEEE binary128. Mapping it to f64 loses precision and mapping it to LongDouble uses the wrong semantic type and potentially the wrong ABI. The configured nightly Rust toolchain provides native f128 behind the f128 feature gate. Clang 24 CIR currently accepts __float128 and emits !cir.f128 but rejects the standard C23 _Float128 spelling even under -std=c23. What: recognize Clang AST and CIR binary128 types, add a distinct Rust AST f128 primitive, emit the required crate feature automatically, lower constants, casts, arithmetic, comparisons, sizeof/alignment, parameters, returns, and storage without narrowing, and add end-to-end differential and generator coverage. Keep quadmath/printf formatting out of scope. Acceptance: a C fixture using Clang's __float128 spelling, Q constants, arithmetic, comparisons, integer/double conversions, function calls, and sizeof/_Alignof translates to Rust containing f128 and #![feature(f128)], compiles, and differentially matches C; _Float128 is recognized by Slate once Clang exposes it as the same AST/CIR type; c.bnf and supported-subset documentation describe the current frontend boundary; cargo fmt, cargo clippy, and cargo nextest r --release pass.
design: Use Rust's native f128 because it maps to LLVM fp128 and preserves binary128 operations on the project's nightly toolchain. Do not reuse f64-backed LongDouble. Gate generated crates with Feature::F128 only when CIR contains binary128. Treat external quadmath functions and printf format idiomatization as follow-up work.
close_reason: Implemented Clang __float128 / CIR !cir.f128 lowering to native nightly Rust f128 with automatic feature gating, exact decimal and 128-bit payload constants, casts/arithmetic/comparisons/calls/layout, effects-model support, differential coverage, generator coverage, grammar, and docs. The C23 _Float128 spelling remains blocked by Clang 24 frontend support and is tracked as slate-pcek.19. cargo fmt --check, clippy -D warnings, and all 690 release nextest tests pass.

title: lower_alloca doesn't disambiguate same-named allocas -- Rust shadowing misdirects an earlier binding's reads/writes
acceptance_criteria: Minimal repro above translates to Rust that type-checks and runs correctly (a == 5, b == 6). tests/fixtures.chibicc/unsupported/alignof/alignof.c's generated Rust has no more same-named-but-differently-typed 'tmp' collisions. Existing differential/chibicc suites stay green; no regression in cases relying on legitimate nested-scope shadowing of repeated names.
close_reason: Same root cause as slate-pcek.4, fixed by the same commit: lower_alloca (src/lower.rs) now dedupes local names per function via a new declared_local_names set / unique_local_name() helper, so distinct hoisted allocas sharing a CIR-generated name (e.g. multiple GNU statement-expression 'tmp' temps) get suffixed (tmp, tmp2, tmp3, ...) instead of colliding into one Rust binding. Verified against this ticket's minimal repro (long/unsigned long statement-expr mix -- now type-checks and returns a==5, b==6) and alignof.c (previously 36 E0308 errors from tmp collisions, now builds clean with zero). Full nextest suite (684 tests) stayed green, including cases with legitimate same-named nested-scope locals, so no shadowing regression. alignof.c still fails end-to-end on an unrelated _Alignas layout bug -- filed separately as slate-pcek.15.

title: chibicc: string.c lowering emits syntactically invalid Rust
description:
Why: tests/fixtures.chibicc/unsupported/string is the most severely broken case found during the chibicc migration triage -- the generated Rust fails with 41 compiler errors including a bare syntax error ('error: expected expression, found .'), not just type mismatches. string.c is dense with string-literal edge cases (escapes, concatenation, wide/UTF string prefixes, indexing into literals). This is likely several distinct bugs bundled in one file.

What: bisect string.c (translate progressively smaller slices, or read the generated Rust directly around the syntax error) to find the specific construct(s) producing malformed Rust syntax -- that is the highest-priority sub-bug since a syntax error blocks even inspecting whether the rest of the file's logic is right.

Acceptance: string.c promotes to supported/, or is split into smaller fixtures.chibicc-independent tests/fixtures/*.c reproductions for each distinct bug found, filed as separate follow-ups if the scope turns out to be more than one issue.
close_reason: Found two distinct bugs, both fixed in src/lower.rs's lower_get_element/global_array_literal_expr: (1) indexing a narrow string literal (e.g. "abc"[0]) decayed the backing global to a single-char pointer before indexing, producing a type error (indexing i8); (2) indexing a wide/concatenated string literal (L""/u"", or narrow+wide concatenation) referenced a const-array global that wasn't in the 'strings' byte map, falling through to a raw unsanitized identifier (e.g. '(*.str.60)[0]') -- a syntax error. Fixed by rendering the backing global as an inline array literal (correctly padded to its declared CIR length, since trailing_zeros initializers omit the padding) and indexing that directly instead of decaying through a pointer. A third, unrelated bug surfaced once those were fixed: stdout line ordering vs C, caused by mixing println! (immediate flush) with raw libc printf (flushes only at exit) across translation units -- fixed in src/fixups/rewrite/printf_format.rs and tracked/documented on slate-pcek.10 since it also unblocked 9 other unsupported fixtures. string.c promoted to tests/fixtures.chibicc/supported/.

title: Wire up Claude Code / Codex cloud routine for beads work
description:
Package a CIR-enabled clang+cir-opt+alive-tv toolchain as a GitHub release asset so a cloud coding-agent (Claude Code cloud routine, or Codex cloud) can pick up 'bd ready' work and open PRs, billed under subscription rather than API usage.

Done:
- scripts/package-toolchain-release.sh: builds/publishes slate-toolchain-linux-x86_64.tar.gz to the 'toolchain' GitHub release tag on Takashiidobe/slate. clang-23/cir-opt were rebuilt inside an ubuntu:24.04 container (glibc 2.38, matching the cloud sandbox OS) rather than the Arch host build (glibc 2.43, incompatible). Only libz3/libhiredis are bundled (alive-tv needs exact SONAMEs apt doesn't provide); glibc-family libs (libc/libm/libgcc_s/libstdc++) are deliberately NOT bundled since they carry ABI markers tied to the target's own libc.so.6.
- scripts/cloud-setup.sh: shared root/Ubuntu-24.04 setup script content, verified end-to-end in a bare 'docker run ubuntu:24.04' — downloads+verifies the toolchain tarball via authenticated 'gh release download', installs bd, smoke-tests all four binaries.

Not done (manual, no tool access to either platform's environment UI):
- Create a Claude Code cloud Environment for Takashiidobe/slate: paste scripts/cloud-setup.sh into its setup-script field, set SLATE_CLANG/SLATE_CIR_OPT/SLATE_ALIVE_TV env vars per the comment at the top of the script.
- Create a matching Codex (ChatGPT) cloud Environment with the same setup script + env vars.
- Once a Claude Code environment_id exists, create the actual routine (RemoteTrigger/schedule skill) telling it to check 'bd ready', follow WORKFLOW.md, and push a branch + open a GitHub PR.
acceptance_criteria: Both a Claude Code cloud routine and a Codex cloud environment can run 'cargo nextest r --release' and produce a differential-tested PR against an open bd issue without manual toolchain setup.
close_reason: Closed

title: _BitInt(128)/unsigned _BitInt(128) misparsed as function types and unrecognized CIR type
description:
Testing i128/u128 support (slate-4bku) surfaced that _BitInt(128)/unsigned _BitInt(128) (C23 bit-precise int spellings, distinct from the __int128 GNU extension) are badly broken, independent of the earlier int_bits width-classification fix (slate-4tbo).

Two separate bugs:
1. c_ast.rs::parse_c_type: _BitInt(128) qualType strings look like RetType(params) to parse_function_qual_type (finds the '(' after _BitInt, treats '_BitInt' as a return type and '128' as a parameter list), so any _BitInt(N) field/local gets misparsed as a function type. Observed: a struct field 's: _BitInt(128)' lowered to 's: Option<fn(i32) -> i32>' -- not even valid Rust.
2. lower.rs: CIR spells _BitInt(128) as a distinct type from __int128 -- '!s128i_bitint'/'!u128i_bitint' (short form) and '!cir.int<s, 128, bitint>'/'!cir.int<u, 128, bitint>' (generic form), not the '!s128i'/'!cir.int<s, 128>' used for __int128. Neither rust_type_with_aliases nor parse_cir_int_type recognized the bitint-suffixed forms, so params/locals/returns of _BitInt(128) type silently fell through to a default of i32.
acceptance_criteria: _BitInt(128) and unsigned _BitInt(128) round-trip correctly as struct fields, locals, params, and returns, verified via differential fixtures comparing C and generated Rust stdout/exit code.
close_reason: Fixed both bugs: (1) c_ast.rs parse_bitint_type now recognizes the whole-string _BitInt(N)/unsigned _BitInt(N) shape before the greedy function-type parsers can misread it; (2) lower.rs rust_type_with_aliases/parse_cir_int_type now recognize !sNi_bitint/!uNi_bitint and !cir.int<s|u, N, bitint> alongside the plain forms. Verified via new differential fixtures bitint128_arith.c/bitint128_struct.c (struct fields, locals, params, returns), full nextest suite, effects_regression, fmt, clippy all green. Committed c5d1aad.

title: Support i128/u128 (__int128 / unsigned __int128) end to end
description:
Slate does not support C's __int128 / unsigned __int128 today. docs/README.md
lists it explicitly under "not handled yet". Investigation
(2026-07-20) found partial scaffolding already exists, apparently added just
to hold oversized CIR constants rather than for a real 128-bit source type:

- rust_ast::Prim already has I128/U128 variants with parse/spelling, and most
  fixups already match them exhaustively.
- The effects interpreter (src/effects/mod.rs) already stores values as i128
  with a separate `signed` flag and has IntWidth::W128.
- CIR width parsing (parse_cir_int_type in lower.rs:7058) is already generic
  over bit-width, so `!s128i`/`!u128i` would already parse correctly.

Gaps still to close:

1. lower.rs::rust_type_with_aliases (~6867): hardcoded if/else chain only
   covers 8/16/32/64-bit CIR type strings (e.g. `!s32i`, `!cir.int<s, 32>`).
   Needs a 128-bit branch mapping to Prim::I128/U128.
2. c_ast.rs::int_bits misclassification of __int128 as 32-bit — tracked
   separately as slate-4tbo; this feature depends on that fix.
3. Unsigned 128-bit constant value representation is the hard part: constant
   storage (RustValue::I128, effects Value::Int) is signed i128, capped below
   u128::MAX. A u128 constant in the top half of its range (above
   i128::MAX) cannot be represented today. Needs either a RustValue::U128 /
   Pattern::U128 variant, or switching storage to a raw 128-bit bit pattern
   plus a signedness flag. parse_cir_int's `.parse::<i128>()` (lower.rs:7462)
   also needs a u128 fallback for values beyond i128::MAX.
4. Fuzzer/differential coverage: c.bnf's <int_type> production and
   tests/support/cgen.rs's fixed-width type emission have no 128-bit
   alternative. Needs a new generator path once lowering supports it, gated
   appropriately (host target / backend must actually support i128/u128
   arithmetic and printf-style output correctly for differential testing to
   be meaningful).
5. docs/README.md's "not handled yet" note needs to drop __int128 once
   support lands, and c.bnf needs the grammar addition documented.
6. AtomicType (rust_ast.rs:412) has no I128/U128 — 128-bit atomics are not
   generally available on target platforms, so scope decision needed: either
   explicitly reject atomic __int128 or leave AtomicType alone and document
   the exclusion.

Not in scope: arbitrary-precision (num-bigint) integer support — there is
none in the codebase today and none is needed; 128-bit bit-pattern storage is
sufficient.
design: Transliterate first: emit #[repr(C)] / raw i128/u128 baseline lowering before any idiomatization. Correctness lives in baseline lowering per project convention, not a fixup.
acceptance_criteria:
- C fixture(s) added under tests/fixtures/ using __int128 and unsigned
  __int128 (arithmetic, comparison, and a printed/returned value spanning
  both halves of the unsigned range).
- CIR -> Rust lowering emits Prim::I128/U128 correctly for 128-bit CIR int
  types (rust_type_with_aliases branch added).
- Constant values across the full unsigned 128-bit range round-trip
  correctly (no silent truncation via i128 parse failure).
- cargo nextest r --release passes, including differential and effects
  regression suites.
- docs/README.md updated to remove __int128 from "not handled yet".
notes: Depends on slate-4tbo (int_bits misclassification) being fixed first, since correct CType::Int{bits}=128 extraction is a prerequisite for correct lowering.
close_reason: Implemented end-to-end: !s128i/!u128i (and generic !cir.int<s|u,128>) lower to Prim::I128/U128 for params, returns, arithmetic, casts, and struct fields. Added RustValue::U128/Pattern::U128 so unsigned constants above i128::MAX round-trip, wired through codegen/effects/fixups. Verified via new fixtures tests/fixtures/int128_arith.c and int128_struct.c passing generated_differential, full nextest suite (639/639), effects_regression, fmt, clippy all green. Committed a308af3. Atomic __int128 confirmed out of scope: ClangIR itself segfaults in CIRGenFunction::emitStmt on _Atomic __int128 before any code/link step (verified independent of -latomic), an upstream ClangIR bug, not fixable from Slate.

title: __int128 misclassified as 32-bit in c_ast::int_bits
description:
c_ast.rs::int_bits (~line 970) determines integer bit-width by string-matching
"char"/"short"/"long" in the C type spelling, defaulting to 32 bits otherwise.
"__int128" and "unsigned __int128" contain none of those substrings, so they
silently fall through to the 32-bit default instead of being recognized as
128-bit. This causes incorrect CType::Int{bits} for any C source using
__int128, independent of whether Slate otherwise supports 128-bit lowering.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Feed a C source declaring a `__int128` (or `unsigned __int128`) variable
   through the Clang AST JSON -> c_ast.rs extraction path.
2. Inspect the resulting CType::Int for that declaration.
3. Observe `bits == 32` instead of `128`.
design: Add an explicit check for "__int128" ahead of/alongside the existing char/short/long substring checks in int_bits, returning 128.
acceptance_criteria: int_bits recognizes "__int128" (and "unsigned __int128") and returns 128; a case/branch exists rather than falling into the generic else. Regression test or unit test added in c_ast.rs covering __int128 type-string parsing.
close_reason: Fixed int_bits to recognize __int128 and _BitInt(N)/unsigned _BitInt(N); verified via full test suite (639/639 pass).

title: Rewrite final returns to tail expressions
description: Add a late no-facts rewrite pass that turns final return expressions at the end of value-returning functions into plain tail expressions, similar to other final cleanup passes.
close_reason: Implemented late no-facts final return tail-expression rewrite with debug pass wiring and updated tests.

title: Add switch-to-match rewrite fixup
description:
Why: with the fact recognizer from slate-04q.59.1 in place, the switch dispatch loop the lowerer always emits (src/lower.rs lower_switch, ~line 5384) can be collapsed to an idiomatic Rust match whenever no case falls through. This is the rewrite half of slate-04q.59, following the same shape as src/fixups/rewrite/goto.rs.

What to do:
- Add src/fixups/rewrite/switch.rs: when the facts layer reports a fallthrough-free switch dispatch loop, replace the Let/Let/Loop scope with a single Stmt::Match (or let-binding + match, matching how other fixups return values) over the original selector expression, using the per-arm (values, body) pairs, with the trailing break 'label stripped from each arm and the default arm using Pattern::Wildcard.
- Register the pass in src/fixups/mod.rs's pipeline (add a Pass variant, wire into the pass list) alongside the other rewrite/ passes.
- Ensure downstream cleanup passes (temp inlining, etc.) still see and clean up match arm bodies the same way they do for other match statements.
- Add fixtures: a fallthrough-free multi-case switch (e.g. the classify() example with break in every case incl. default) and confirm output is a direct match with no loop/label. Add/keep a fallthrough fixture that confirms the loop form is left untouched.
- Update docs/idiomatization.md or docs/passes.md describing the recovered shape and the fallthrough-free precondition, per WORKFLOW.md's rule to keep docs in sync with lowerer/fixup behavior.

Acceptance criteria:
- Fallthrough-free switch fixtures lower to a genuine match expression, not a labeled dispatch loop.
- Fallthrough fixtures still produce the existing correct loop/dispatch form (fixup is a no-op there).
- cargo nextest r --release (differential + effects regression) passes.
- cargo fmt clean; docs updated.
acceptance_criteria: Fallthrough-free switches lower to a direct match instead of the __switch loop; fallthrough switches are untouched by the new pass and still lower correctly; full nextest suite and effects regression pass; docs describe the recovered shape.
notes: Second half of the switch-to-match recovery in slate-04q.59, depends on the fact recognizer in slate-04q.59.1. Mirrors slate-04q.40.11 (goto_structure rewrite fixup).
close_reason: Added src/fixups/rewrite/switch.rs: collapses fallthrough-free __switch_value/__switch_case dispatch loops into a direct match over the selector. Registered Pass::Switch in trace.rs (all four sites), wired into apply_with_logger immediately after Pass::Goto, documented in docs/passes.md as pipeline step 2. Eligibility requires fallthrough_free plus each non-default case having exactly one originating value (grouped C case labels always lower with an intermediate fallthrough hop under current baseline lowering, so they're correctly excluded, not silently mishandled). Default case (or absence of one) becomes the match's trailing wildcard arm for exhaustiveness. 3 new unit tests plus differential coverage via switch_default.c/switch_no_default.c/switch_sparse.c/switch_loop_control.c (already-existing fixtures, now exercising the new pass); switch_fallthrough.c confirms the loop form is left untouched. Full suite: 629/635 passing, same 6 pre-existing failures as before this change.

title: Recognize fallthrough-free switch dispatch loop shape in fixup facts
description:
Why: the switch-to-match rewrite (slate-04q.59) needs a fact layer that recognizes the canonical __switch_valueN/__switch_caseN loop the lowerer emits (src/lower.rs lower_switch, ~line 5384) and determines whether it's safe to collapse to a plain match — i.e. no case arm uses the case_name = index + 1; continue 'label fallthrough trick. Follows the precedent of src/fixups/facts/goto.rs, which does the equivalent recognition for the goto dispatch loop.

What to do:
- Add a recognizer (e.g. src/fixups/facts/switch.rs) that, given a Stmt::Scope/Loop body, identifies the switch dispatch shape: a Let binding the selector, a Let building a case index via Expr::Match on the selector, and a labeled Stmt::Loop containing a single Stmt::Match on the case index.
- Extract, per case arm: the originating selector constant(s) (from the first match's arms), the arm body, and whether the arm ends in break 'label (terminal) or the continue-with-reassignment fallthrough pattern.

title: Recover switch dispatch loops as idiomatic match expressions
description:
Why: cir.switch always lowers to a __switch_value/__switch_case dispatch loop (src/lower.rs lower_switch, ~line 5384) — a labeled loop wrapping a match on a synthetic case index, with case bodies ending in either break 'label or, for C fallthrough, case_name = index + 1; continue 'label. That loop form is necessary as a correctness fallback because fallthrough can't be expressed by a plain Rust match arm falling into the next arm. But the large majority of real switches never fall through, and for those the loop/label/index-match machinery is pure noise versus a direct match x { 1 => ..., 2 => ..., _ => ... }.

This mirrors slate-04q.40 (goto): keep the general dispatch-loop lowering as the correctness fallback, and add a fixup that recognizes the fallthrough-free case and rewrites it to an idiomatic match, leaving the loop form untouched whenever fallthrough (or anything else non-trivial) is present.

What to do:
- Add fact-gathering (likely src/fixups/facts/, alongside goto.rs's precedent) to recognize the canonical __switch_valueN/__switch_caseN loop shape and determine whether any case arm uses the continue-based fallthrough trick.
- Add a rewrite fixup (src/fixups/rewrite/, e.g. switch.rs) that, when fallthrough-free, fuses the selector match and the dispatch match into a single match on the original selector expression, drops the trailing break 'label from each arm, and removes the now-unused loop/label wrapper.
- Wire the new pass into the fixup pipeline (src/fixups/mod.rs) alongside goto/singleton_scopes-style cleanups.
- Leave the loop form untouched (fixup no-ops) whenever any case falls through, matching the 'disabling it still leaves correct Rust' rule.

Acceptance criteria:
- Non-fallthrough switch fixtures (e.g. a classify()-style switch with break in every case, including default) lower to a genuine Rust match, not a labeled loop.
- Fallthrough switch fixtures still lower via the existing dispatch-loop fallback and remain correct.
- Differential tests (cargo nextest r --release) and effects regression stay green.
- docs/idiomatization.md or docs/passes.md documents the recovered switch-to-match shape and its fallthrough-free precondition.
acceptance_criteria: Fallthrough-free switches emit a direct Rust match instead of the __switch loop/dispatch form; fallthrough switches still lower correctly via the existing loop fallback; differential and effects-regression suites stay green; the boundary is documented.
notes: Follow-up from discussion in this session: example was classify(x) with break in every case (tests/fixtures-style), showing the __switch_value0/__switch_case0 loop form. Sibling epic to slate-04q.40 (goto dispatch-loop cleanup) — same philosophy, same precedent (src/fixups/rewrite/goto.rs).

- complex.c: "expected int operand, found Ref(Location{...})" — a complex-number op is receiving a pointer/ref where an int operand was expected (likely real/imag component extraction gone through a ref instead of a direct field read).
- vector_extension_ops.c: "read of unknown scalar `_v1`" — a compiler-generated vector-extension temp isn't bound before use.
- varargs.c: "user function `sum` expected 2 arg(s), got 5" — variadic user-function calls aren't binding extra varargs into the callee; arg-count checking assumes a fixed arity.
- volatile_qualified_types.c: "expected int operand, found Float(4.0)" — a volatile-qualified float local/op is falling into an integer-operand code path.
- array_types.c: "expected array local, found Array{elem:Prim(F64), len:3}" — array-of-double locals aren't recognized as array locals (likely an f64-specific gap in the array-local lookup).
- comments.c: "unknown type `Mode` in size_of" — a user enum type isn't registered for size_of.
- target_stack_builtin_ops.c: "expected an integer value, found Null" — a stack/frame builtin (e.g. __builtin_frame_address/alloca-adjacent) is producing a Null value where an integer was expected.
- destructor_early_return.c: "unsupported method `collect`" — a .collect() call (likely from an array/iterator-based destructor-cleanup rewrite) has no method summary.

title: Effects: investigate array_init.c raw-vs-fixuped alloc-id divergence
description:
array_init.c is a trace divergence, not an extraction failure: both raw and fixuped rust_ast interpret successfully, but at effect #19 the same printf call references different AllocIds for what should be the same logical string literal allocation (AllocId(2) on raw side vs AllocId(4) on fixuped side).

Per docs/effects.md's Normalization section, 'allocation id shifts caused by unobserved allocations' are exactly the kind of representation-only difference the comparator should normalize away — this looks like that case landing on a live (observed, printf-referenced) allocation instead of an unobserved one, so the existing normalization doesn't catch it.

Before adding a blanket normalization: confirm the two allocations really do hold identical bytes/contents (i.e. this is a benign numbering artifact from the fixup pass introducing/removing an earlier allocation) and not a real fixup bug that changed which string gets printed.

Reproduce:
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/array_init.c
acceptance_criteria: Either: (a) confirmed benign — comparator normalizes matching-content allocations referenced by the same logical call site regardless of AllocId, and array_init.c passes; or (b) confirmed real bug — the fixup pass is fixed so both sides reference the same source string, and array_init.c passes without new normalization.
close_reason: Investigated with a concrete repro (thanks to user-supplied C/Rust source). Confirmed root cause by reading src/effects/rust_ast/interp.rs: call_printf()/print() push raw Value::Ref(Location) for %s-style string arguments into Effect::Call, comparing pointer identity rather than resolving to printed byte content. array_init.c's divergence (padded's %s arg: raw side refs the real buffer AllocId(3), fixuped side refs a freshly-minted AllocId(4) for a substituted string literal with identical bytes) is the same root cause already tracked in slate-tpz.20 (printf/format argument evaluation), which now carries the full mechanism and fix direction. Folded into slate-tpz.20 rather than tracked separately, since one fix (resolve %s args to bytes at Call-construction time) should close both.

title: Effects: model function/callable values as raw rust_ast scalars
description:
3 fixtures fail on raw rust_ast with "read of unknown scalar `<name>`" where the name is actually a function/callable identifier, not a plain local:

- function_pointer_presence.c: unknown scalar `bump` (a function name used as a value, e.g. assigned to a function-pointer-typed variable or compared/printed).
- function_pointers.c: unknown scalar `add_pair` (same pattern — function used as a first-class value).
- libyaml_type_shapes.c: unknown scalar `read_bytes` — likely a function or closure-shaped field being read as a value rather than called.

The interpreter currently only knows how to *call* a named user function (via the generic call-dispatch path from slate-tpz.2); it doesn't have a value representation for "this identifier names a function" so that the identifier can be read, stored, and later invoked indirectly.

Reproduce:
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/function_pointer_presence.c
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/function_pointers.c
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/libyaml_type_shapes.c
acceptance_criteria: A bare reference to a function name evaluates to a function-pointer Value (not an unknown-scalar error), usable as a struct/local value and callable through the existing generic call path when invoked indirectly. All 3 listed fixtures pass.
notes: touches: src/effects/mod.rs, src/effects/interp.rs, tests/effects_regression.rs
close_reason: Implemented first-class effects Function values, Option<fn> storage/unwrapping, indirect user-call dispatch, and call-frame scalar_locs shadowing. Verified with cargo fmt, cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features, the three compare-effects-rust-rust acceptance commands, and cargo nextest r --release --test effects_regression function_pointer_values_preserve_rust_effects libc_resource_shims_preserve_rust_effects. Full effects regression is 19/20; all-fixture ratchet improved to 158 passed / 14 failed with remaining failures covered by sibling beads.

description:

title: Effects: model Vec/slice/Box std-idiom summaries introduced by fixups
description:
6 fixtures fail on the fixuped rust_ast side because fixup passes rewrite raw libc/pointer code into std idioms the interpreter doesn't evaluate yet:

- heap_box_fixup.c: "unsupported call target `Box::<i32>::new`" — the box fixup rewrites a heap alloc into Box::new; no call summary for it.
- stdio_fread_multi_byte.c, stdio_fread_short_read.c, stdio_fread_size_one.c: "unsupported call target `Vec::new`" — the fread fixup allocates a Vec<u8> buffer instead of a raw pointer; Vec::new (and presumably push/resize/as_slice) has no summary.
- stdio_fwrite_return.c: "unsupported write_all bytes `Unsafe(Block{... Call std::slice::from_raw_parts(buf.as_ptr(), _v8 as usize * _v9 as usize) })`" — write_all's byte-slice argument is an unsafe block building a slice from a raw pointer + computed length; the interpreter needs to evaluate that expression down to bytes rather than reject the whole write_all node.
- string_libc_fixup.c: "unsupported method `split_at`" — the string fixup pass rewrites raw strchr/strstr-style code to str::split_at; no method summary.

Reproduce:
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/heap_box_fixup.c
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/stdio_fread_multi_byte.c
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/stdio_fwrite_return.c
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/string_libc_fixup.c
acceptance_criteria: Box::new, Vec::new (plus whatever Vec methods the fread fixup emits), write_all over an unsafe-from_raw_parts slice expression, and str::split_at all evaluate to the same observable effects as their raw-side counterparts. All 6 listed fixtures pass.
notes: Implemented std-idiom effects coverage for Box::new, Vec::new/read_to_end/copy_nonoverlapping, unsafe std::slice::from_raw_parts write_all bytes, split_at byte comparisons, and string find/rfind/contains idioms. Verification: six listed compare-effects-rust-rust fixtures pass; cargo nextest r --release --test effects_regression std_idiom_fixups_preserve_rust_effects passes. Broad effects_regression all-fixture ratchet after this change: 151 passed, 21 failed; remaining failures are unrelated raw extraction gaps tracked by sibling slate-tpz beads.
close_reason: Implemented std idiom effects summaries and focused regression. Verified six listed compare-effects-rust-rust fixtures plus cargo nextest r --release --test effects_regression std_idiom_fixups_preserve_rust_effects.

title: Effects: raw rust_ast memory ops through void*-cast PtrCopy/WriteBytes and realloc summary
description:
4 fixtures fail on the raw rust_ast side around bulk memory ops:

- mem_bcopy_overlap.c: "unsupported expr PtrCopy{ src: Cast(Cast(ArrayPtr(buf), *mut c_void), *const u8), dst: Cast(Cast(MethodCall(ArrayPtr(buf).add(2)), *mut c_void), *mut u8), count: ..., overlapping: true }" — PtrCopy is only recognized when src/dst are directly typed pointers, not when routed through an intermediate void* cast (the shape memmove/bcopy-style lowering produces).
- mem_bitcast_copy.c: same PtrCopy-through-void* shape but with AddrOf(local) endpoints instead of ArrayPtr.
- mem_bzero.c: "unsupported expr WriteBytes{ dst: Cast(Cast(ArrayPtr(a), *mut c_void), *mut u8), val: ..., count: ... }" — same void*-cast issue but for WriteBytes (bzero-style lowering).
- heap_vec_realloc.c: "unsupported call target `realloc`" — realloc has no call summary; the doc's memory-call summary list (malloc/free/memcpy/memmove/memset/memchr) is missing it.

This is a general pattern: PtrCopy/WriteBytes destination/source resolution should peel through Cast(..., *mut/const c_void) wrappers to find the underlying pointer place, the same way AddrOf(Index(...)) is already handled per docs/effects.md.

Reproduce:
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/mem_bcopy_overlap.c
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/mem_bitcast_copy.c
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/mem_bzero.c
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/heap_vec_realloc.c
acceptance_criteria: PtrCopy/WriteBytes resolve their src/dst through void*-cast wrappers for both ArrayPtr and AddrOf(local) endpoints. realloc gets a call summary consistent with malloc/free (updates modeled allocation size, preserves/copies existing bytes). All 4 listed fixtures pass.
close_reason: Implemented raw rust_ast PtrCopy/WriteBytes execution through casted pointer expressions, aggregate copy handling, realloc/Vec resize summaries, and fixture regressions. Verified with cargo fmt, cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features, four compare-effects-rust-rust acceptance commands, and cargo nextest r --release --test effects_regression raw_memory_ops_through_void_casts_preserve_rust_effects libc_resource_shims_preserve_rust_effects.

title: Effects: printf/format pointer signedness and char/string argument evaluation
description:
5 fixtures diverge or fail in formatted-output argument evaluation. Root cause (confirmed by reading src/effects/rust_ast/interp.rs: call_printf() at line ~3842 and print() at line ~1061): both raw-printf and fixed-println!/print! call sites evaluate each format argument with the generic self.eval(arg) and push the resulting Value straight into Effect::Call{args}. For a %s/string argument this yields Value::Ref(Location) — the *pointer identity*, not the bytes it points to. The comparator (src/effects/interpreter.rs) never resolves a Ref arg down to its pointed-to string content; it only compares Locations after alloc-id compaction (compact_alloc_map) and an all-or-nothing externally_observable_projection fallback. So whenever a fixup changes *how* a string's bytes are produced for a %s call — reusing the original buffer's location vs. introducing a brand-new literal/location with the same bytes — the AllocId differs and comparison fails, even though the printed output would be byte-identical.

- printf_pointer.c, printf_pointer_rejected.c: trace diverges at #0 — same printf call, same integer value (4660), but one side is Int{signed:false} and the other Int{signed:true} for a pointer-as-integer format argument (likely %p / pointer-to-int cast). Needs consistent (unsigned, matching C's uintptr_t semantics) signedness on both raw and fixuped sides.
- printf_string_char.c: trace diverges at #0 — raw side passes bare Int args (65, 10, 7) where fixuped side passes Ref(Location) args for the same positions — a %c/%s argument is being modeled as a scalar on one side and a pointer/reference on the other. Same root cause as array_init.c below.
- printf_alternate_integer.c (fixuped side): "unsupported expr Macro { name: "format", args: [Str("{:#x}"), Var(...)] }" — the format!() macro node isn't interpreted at all yet.
- array_init.c (formerly tracked separately as slate-tpz.27, folded in here — same root cause): trace diverges at #19. C declares `char padded[8] = "hi";` then `printf("%s %d\n", padded, padded[4]);`. Raw lowering keeps `padded` as a real byte buffer (AllocId 3) and the printf %s arg is Ref(alloc3). The string_libc-style fixup statically determines padded's printed bytes never change and substitutes the Rust string literal "hi" directly into println! args instead of routing through the padded local — this mints a brand-new, unrelated AllocId(4) for the literal (no explicit Alloc effect, just a fresh id from eval() constructing a Location for the literal) purely to have something Ref-able. Both sides print "hi" — this is NOT a real fixup bug — but Ref(alloc3) != Ref(alloc4) as raw Values, so the trace comparator reports a divergence. (Note: the earlier %s print of `s`/"hello" in the same fixture happens to NOT diverge, purely because both sides mint their string-holding AllocId in the same position in allocation order — that is coincidence, not a working case.)

The real fix belongs in argument resolution, not comparator normalization: call_printf()/print() should resolve %s/string-typed arguments to their actual byte content (dereference C string args to bytes-until-NUL; &str/literal args to their known bytes) when constructing the Call effect, rather than leaving a live Value::Ref(Location) to be compared by pointer identity. That single change should fix printf_string_char.c and array_init.c simultaneously, and is the kind of interpreter-side resolution the docs/effects.md formatted-output guidance already calls for ("the target model is stdout/stderr bytes, not both sides called printf").

Reproduce:
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/printf_pointer.c
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/printf_pointer_rejected.c
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/printf_string_char.c
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/printf_alternate_integer.c
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/array_init.c
acceptance_criteria: All five fixtures pass. Pointer-valued printf args have consistent signedness across raw/fixuped traces. %s/string-typed format arguments (printf and println!/print!) resolve to their actual byte content at Call-effect-construction time instead of comparing by Location/AllocId identity, so fixups that change a string's underlying storage (buffer vs. literal) without changing its printed bytes no longer cause spurious divergence. format!()/write! macro exprs are evaluated to their expanded output bytes rather than rejected.
close_reason: Closed

title: Effects: model libc stdout/stderr FILE* globals in raw rust_ast
description:
5 fixtures fail on raw rust_ast with "read of unknown scalar `stdout`": stdio_file_ownership.c, stdio_file_write.c, stdio_gets_loop_eof.c, stdio_gets_loop_lines.c, stdio_gets_loop_truncation.c.

The raw lowered Rust references the libc `stdout` (and presumably `stderr`) FILE* global directly (e.g. passed to fwrite/fputs), and the interpreter has no binding for it as a known scalar/location — it's not a user local, so eval_call/eval falls through to the unknown-scalar-read error path.

Reproduce:
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/stdio_file_write.c

Note this is the raw side specifically — fixuped Rust presumably goes through a resource-shim path already covered by slate-tpz.14, but raw lowering's direct libc FILE* globals are a separate gap.
acceptance_criteria: stdout/stderr are recognized as well-known FILE* globals (their own File/stream location) usable directly in raw rust_ast, without requiring a fixup pass first. All 5 listed fixtures pass compare-effects-rust-rust.
close_reason: Registered stdout/stderr as reserved FILE* handles (STDOUT_FILE/STDERR_FILE) in src/effects/rust_ast/interp.rs: seed_program now binds extern-static stdout/stderr from ExternBlock decls directly into scalars/files, and file_arg recognizes std::io::stdout()/stderr() calls for the fixuped side's write_all rewrite. Added 2 focused unit tests (stdout_extern_static_reads_as_reserved_file_handle, write_all_to_std_io_stdout_call_targets_reserved_file_handle). Ratchet: 141->143 passed, 31->29 failed (cargo fmt, cargo nextest r --release: 637/637 green). stdio_file_ownership.c and stdio_file_write.c now fully pass compare-effects-rust-rust as required. The other 3 listed fixtures (stdio_gets_loop_eof/lines/truncation) no longer fail on the stdout scalar — their raw side now passes — but their fixuped side hits a separate, previously-undiscovered gap: the fgets-loop fixup rewrites into std::io::BufReader::new/BufRead::read_until, which the interpreter doesn't model. Filed and linked slate-l0x for that gap; out of scope for this bead's stdout/stderr FILE* global goal.

title: Effects: atomic pointer-cast places, global registration, and signedness
description:
all_fixtures_preserve_rust_effects_through_fixups (raw rust_ast side) fails on 4 fixtures around atomics:

- atomic_fallbacks.c: unsupported atomic pointer place `Cast { expr: AddrOf { mutable: true, expr: Var(Ident("p")) }, ty: Ptr { mutable: true, inner: Prim(I64) } }` — atomic op through a cast-to-pointer of a plain local, not just AddrOf directly.
- atomic_flag_ops.c: same shape but through a struct field (`_Value`) — `Cast { expr: AddrOf { mutable: true, expr: Field { base: Var(Ident("flag")), field: "_Value" } }, ... }`.
- atomic_widths.c: trace diverges at #0 — AtomicRmw operand/old/new are unsigned on one side (signed: false) and signed on the other (signed: true) for the same width/value. Likely a signedness-preservation bug in atomic RMW modeling, not a missing shape.
- type_qualifiers.c: "atomic access to unknown `atomic_counter`" — a top-level `_Atomic` qualified global isn't being registered as an atomic location at all.

Reproduce:
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/atomic_fallbacks.c
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/atomic_flag_ops.c
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/atomic_widths.c
  cargo run -- compare-effects-rust-rust tests/fixtures/type_qualifiers.c
acceptance_criteria: All four fixtures pass compare-effects-rust-rust. atomic pointer places recognized through Cast(AddrOf(local-or-field)); atomic_counter-style qualified globals registered as atomic locations at extraction time; AtomicRmw preserves the source signedness on both old/new/operand.
close_reason: Fixed all 4 target fixtures (atomic_fallbacks.c, atomic_flag_ops.c, atomic_widths.c, type_qualifiers.c) in compare-effects-rust-rust. Root causes: (1) atomic pointer places only recognized AddrOf directly, not Cast(AddrOf(...)) or struct-field targets; (2) AtomicRmw operand/old/new defaulted to signed i32 instead of the declared AtomicType's width/signedness; (3) _Atomic-qualified globals accessed via from_ptr weren't resolved through the global/heap registry, and the comparator had no AtomicId canonicalization (mirroring the existing AllocId compaction), so eager (fixuped) vs lazy (raw) atomic bootstrap order caused spurious id mismatches. Added an AtomicBacking write-through so from_ptr-viewed atomics (a view over existing storage, not a replacement) keep plain scalar/field reads in sync. Verified: all 4 fixtures pass; effects_regression ratchet improved 137->141 passed (35->31 failed) with the same pre-existing 31 failures (e.g. mt-atomics.c) untouched -- no regressions. Merged into main via --no-ff; cargo fmt clean; full cargo nextest r --release (635 tests) passes.

Part of slate-m6e. src/lower.rs has ~318 op.name.as_str() match sites (by far the largest single consumer) dispatching CIR ops to Rust AST lowering. Migrate them to match on CirOpKind instead of raw string literals, once the enum exists (depends on the core definition ticket).
